data.addressing-a-build#Addressing a build:
A version is not an address. fftw.org@3.3.11 built with CUDA and the same version built without it are two different things that run differently, and anything that calls them both 3.3.11 has to pick one and hope.
go-zpkg gives every build an identity — a hash of what it is — and puts that identity in both places a build is named: its directory in the store, and its tag in the registry.
store /fftw.org/v3.3.11-h7k2mq4xvbnd3rf5c registry ghcr.io/…/fftw.org:3.3.11-h7k2mq4xvbnd3rf5c What ships today. The identity, the hashed store prefix, the hashed registry tag and the spec annotation are in zbk v0.63.0 and bottle v0.81.0, and zbk factory publishes with them. zpkgs builds is in zpkgx v0.36.0 and runs now.
What does not. Naming a build with @version/ is refused by the resolver rather than honoured: carrying the hash down to the store is zpkgx#142. Running some build of a version under a name that says you chose one would be worse than saying no, so it says no and points at zpkgs builds.
And until the registry is rebuilt with hashed tags, every published bottle answers nothing recorded — which is the truth about the registry as it stands, not a defect in the command.
data.listing#Listing the builds of a version:
When more than one build of a version exists, the resolver refuses rather than choosing:
fftw.org 3.3.11 was published as 2 different builds and nothing here says which: a variant hash is not a version, so there is no newest one to pick That refusal is only half a design without a way to answer it:
$ zpkgs builds fftw.org@3.3.11 HASH INSTALLED PUBLISHED SIGNED BY WHAT 27o3ysxva6swayci - yes go-zpkg ⚠ withdrawn: CVE-2026-1234 → rnp44i · go.dev 1.27.3/aaaaaa rnp44isdgdtzxcit - yes go-zpkg, alice go.dev 1.27.4/bbbbbb One list joining the store and the registry, because a list of only what is installed cannot answer what else could I have, and a list of only what is published cannot answer what do I already have.
data.naming-one#Naming one:
A build is named by appending any prefix of its hash to the version, after a slash — fftw.org@3.3.11/7k2mq4.
/ is Spack’s spelling, borrowed on purpose. Its manual: “In place of a spec in any command, substitute / where is any amount from the beginning of a spec hash.” It is the one form that works without knowing a package’s variant vocabulary — which matters most exactly when a refusal has just handed you two hashes and you have to pick.
Any prefix of the hash will do, as long as it names exactly one build. If it matches two, that is a question rather than a choice, and you are told so with both candidates listed so the next attempt can be longer.
The @version is required before the hash. A project name contains slashes — a third of the pantry is named that way — so x.org/pciaccess has to stay a project name. The syntax decides, not the shape of the trailing component: without an @version in front of it, a trailing component is part of the project name, always.
data.no-unhashed-path#Why there is no unhashe:
There is no //v beside the hashed directories, and no v1 / v1.2 / v* alias either — not even as a symlink, because a symlink is a path too.
The break tells that story in full: the aliases were inherited from pkgx, they only ever advanced, and installing an older line of a project silently demoted v2 onto it, so every consumer bound to v2 loaded the older library. The fix was careful, and it was a careful fix to a problem created by having the alias at all.
data.ordering#Ordering them:
--sort=status|closure|hash|installed.
closure is the one a reader means by “newer”: a build made against a later toolchain first. It is the comparison a CVE rebuild creates — a Go patch release fixes a standard-library defect, nothing about the recipe or the upstream version changes, only go.dev in the closure.
It is a partial order. One build is later than another only when it is at least as new on every dependency they share and strictly newer on one. Two builds that each lead on a different dependency are genuinely incomparable, and declaring a winner would invent an order; they tie, and the tie falls back to the hash. A build that gained a dependency the other does not have is a different shape, not a later version of it — the CUDA build does not supersede the plain one.
There is no date key, and that is a property rather than a gap. A published bottle’s timestamp is pinned — zbk factory stamps SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, or its own fixed epoch, never the wall clock — so that re-publishing the same bottle yields byte-identical attestations and the same referrer digests, which is what makes a re-push idempotent instead of accumulating duplicates.
Every bottle therefore carries the same instant. Sorting by it would order a list by a constant while looking like it ordered by time, and taking the wall clock instead would make every rebuild a new artefact.
--sort=installed orders by when this machine got them, which is a fact about your disk and not about the builds.
data.signed-by-column#The SIGNED BY column:
Two builders who build the same inputs get the same hash — deliberately — so what tells them apart is who put their key on the result. The column names them as your own trust set names them, never as the registry does: a name on the artefact is written by whoever pushed it.
A ⚠ marks a row that does not meet your ZPKG_TRUST_THRESHOLD and will be refused at install time. A ? means the registry could not be asked, which is not the same as nobody signed it — rendering the two alike is how a network failure becomes a claim about the artefact. See Supply chain.
data.tag-and-annotation#The tag carries the a:
A hash is opaque by construction. Nix pays for that: a store path says which build and never what build, so answering “the one with CUDA?” needs a second index.
So a published bottle carries its spec on its manifest:
io.github.go-zpkg.spec = {"v":1,"platform":"linux/x86-64","deps":[…],"recipe":"sha256:…"} and a reader recomputes the hash from it and checks it against the tag. An identity you cannot recompute is a claim, not a description; both halves come from whoever could push to the registry, so reading the second without checking it against the first would let a bottle tagged as the plain build describe itself as the CUDA one.
Spack keeps the spec queryable the same way (spack find libdwarf +debug), and conda writes its hash inputs to info/hash_input.json beside the hash. Readability is a tooling property here, not a naming one.
A bottle that was only mirrored carries neither: no hash in its tag and no annotation. We do not know how it was built, and a tag claiming an address would say we do.
data.views#Defaults live outside the store:
A default version is not a property of the store. The store holds builds, each at its own hashed path, and nothing in it says which one you prefer.
A default is a view: a directory of symlinks pointing into the store, written where the chooser lives rather than where the builds live.
That separation is what makes the following work at once:
A shared store on NFS can be mounted read-only and still serve a site. Each user’s default is in their own profile, and choosing one writes nothing into the shared tree. A container or microVM built from an environment computes its links at creation time from the shared store, so the image gets exactly the builds that environment resolved — not whatever the host happened to default to. Two environments on one machine can prefer different builds of one version without either of them winning. Nix makes the same separation with profiles, and for the same reason: “One cannot copy a store object to a store with a different store directory” — a cache stops being shareable the moment identity depends on where the reader keeps it. The install prefix is therefore not part of the hash.
data.what-column#The WHAT column is the whole:
A column of bare hashes is unusable. A hash is opaque by construction, so a list of two of them hands the reader back the problem the command was asked to solve.
So each row says what differs — not what the build is. A full spec is fifty-odd dependencies identical in all but one, and printing it per row buries the one that matters. The axes are computed across all the builds first, so two rows cannot describe themselves on different axes and read as two unrelated facts rather than a comparison.
When nothing else differs, the recipe is named: a rebuild after a pantry edit is one of the commonest reasons two builds of a version exist, and it is invisible in the closure. With nothing printed those rows would be identical and the list would look broken.
A build nothing records says nothing recorded rather than showing a blank cell, which reads as a rendering fault.
A registry that could not be reached is an error, not an empty list — an unobtained answer must not read as “nothing is published”, because that is how you conclude a build does not exist and rebuild it. What is installed is still listed alongside the error: it is a true answer to half the question, and it needs no network.
data.what-the-hash-is-of#What the hash is of:
The platform, the resolved closure — every dependency at the exact version and build it was made against — and a digest of the recipe.
Three consequences follow, and they are the reason it is built this way.
It is a function of the inputs, never of the output. The prefix is baked into every binary the build produces, so it has to be known before a compiler runs. Hashing the result into the result is circular. Nix hashes the derivation and Spack the concrete DAG for the same reason.
It is Merkle, for free. A dependency is identified by the prefix it resolved to, and that prefix carries the dependency’s own hash — so hashing the edge carries the whole dependency with it, transitively. It is the mechanism Nix uses when a derivation references its inputs by store path.
The recipe reaches it as a digest of the parsed value, not of the file. Reformatting a recipe, reordering its keys or rewriting its comments does not move the hash; changing what it says does. Hashing the file’s bytes instead would make a reflowed comment rebuild the world — every dependent’s hash moves, every bottle is republished, and no binary differs. Spack strips comments and docstrings from package.py before hashing for the same reason.
data.withdrawing#Withdrawing a build:
When a CVE catches a build, ZPKG_WITHDRAWN names a JSON file saying so:
{"fftw.org": [{"version": "3.3.11", "hash": "27o3ysxva6swayci", "because": "CVE-2026-1234", "superseded_by": "rnp44isdgdtzxcit"}]} A build, not a version — and that is the point. When the flaw is in the toolchain a package was compiled with, the package is fine, the source is fine, and the fix is another build of the same version. That is only nameable because a build has an identity; it is the first thing this layout buys that a version-addressed store could not do at all.
It ranks, it does not filter. A withdrawn build stays resolvable:
two builds, one withdrawn → the other, and the withdrawal is announced; one build, withdrawn → that one, loudly, because there is nothing else; several left after the withdrawn ones are set aside → still ambiguous. The reasoning is the same as for end-of-life release lines: a lock pins a build, and a lock that stops resolving is a worse defect than the one being fixed. Reproducibility and an explicit request outrank the preference.
An entry with no hash withdraws every build of the version — a flaw in the source rather than in how it was compiled — and an entry naming one build wins over it, so the build that fixes the flaw is not reported as carrying it.
The list is read locally and never from the network: the resolver must keep working FROM scratch and air-gapped. Where the file comes from — zbk advisories and the VEX documents attached to published bottles — is a separate matter.

data.build-isolation#Build isolation: Packages are only as trustworthy as the environment that produced them. The factory builds in two phases, one shipped and one experimental.
data.phase-a-debian-container-shipped#Phase A:
Builds run inside a pinned debian:stable-slim container rather than on the drifting GitHub-runner host. This gives:
a controlled, known glibc floor instead of whatever the runner ships; no host-tool leakage into the build — only the declared base plus zpkgx-sourced dependencies are present; reproducible output across runs. This is the isolation model in use for every published package today.
data.phase-b-from-scratch-zpkgx-glibc-toolcha:
Phase A still links against the container’s glibc. Phase B goes further: build against zpkgx’s own glibc toolchain so packages are truly self-contained and run on a literally-empty FROM scratch base with no system libc at all.
It is shipped, and it is the default. The factory’s sovereign input says so in its own description: blank builds inside the FROM scratch rootfs bk builder stages, “so neither the host’s libc nor its compiler takes part”, and 0 is what falls back to the runner’s distribution.
bk build --libc=zpkgx and bk factory --libc=zpkgx target the gnu.org/glibc bottle — its crt objects, its libc, its dynamic linker — instead of the container’s; --glibc pins that sysroot to an exact glibc line; bk builder stages the rootfs itself: static Go binaries plus toolchain bottles from the signed registry, nothing else; design note: bk/docs/from-scratch-toolchain.md. Corrected 2026-10-27. This page previously described Phase B as experimental, living on branch feat/zpkgx-glibc-toolchain, and gated behind a BK_ZPKG_LIBC=1 environment variable. All three were out of date: the work is on main, the gate is the --libc flag above, and BK_ZPKG_LIBC appears nowhere in bk’s code — only inside the design note that first proposed it.
data.what-a-sovereign-toolchain-does-not-reac:
The sysroot, the -isystem directories and the runtime choice reach a build through the compiler driver — cc, which is bk’s own shim and re-execs $BK_CC, or $CC. A tool that drives the compiler some other way sees none of it.
bindgen is that tool: it calls libclang in-process. A Rust crate generating bindings therefore got the container’s idea of a libc, or none at all —
/zpkgx/openssl.org/v3.6.4/include/openssl/asn1.h:27:10: fatal error: 'stdio.h' file not found — in a build where openssl 3.6.4 had been found, probed and configured correctly a few lines earlier. Since bk v0.43.0 sovereign mode also exports BINDGEN_EXTRA_CLANG_ARGS, the variable bindgen’s own documentation names for exactly this, carrying the header-finding flags only and appended to whatever the recipe set.
See Running pkgx packages on FROM scratch for why a system-linked package needs closure completion to run on scratch, and what Phase B removes.

data.converting-a-sites-modulefiles#Convertin:
zpkgs env import reads Lmod’s Lua and Environment Modules’ TCL, and writes both into the same HCL2.
$ zpkgs env import /opt/modulefiles/hdf5 # imported from /opt/modulefiles/hdf5 by `zpkgs env import`. # Every statement in that file was recognised; nothing was skipped. env "hdf5" { description = "HDF5 1.14.3" prepend_path = { LD_LIBRARY_PATH = ["/opt/hdf5/1.14.3/lib"] PATH = ["/opt/hdf5/1.14.3/bin"] } setenv = { HDF5_DIR = "/opt/hdf5/1.14.3" } } It is a parser, not an evaluator. An interpreter runs a modulefile and silently skips what it does not implement; the result is not an error but an environment that is subtly wrong, found later inside somebody’s job. This refuses anything it would have to guess at, names the line, and — the part that matters — writes nothing at all if any file was refused, because a partial conversion is the one outcome nobody can check.
$ zpkgs env import /opt/modulefiles/openmpi.lua /opt/modulefiles/hdf5 /opt/modulefiles/openmpi.lua: 3 statement(s) this converter will not guess at: line 3: not a plain call: this converter reads statements, it does not run Lua local root = "/opt/openmpi/5.0.8" line 4: argument is not a string literal (pathJoin(root, "bin")): its value depends on something we are not running prepend_path("PATH", pathJoin(root, "bin")) line 5: depends_on states a RELATIONSHIP between modules, not an environment change: decide it in the environment that replaces this one depends_on("hwloc") zpkgs: 1 of 2 modulefile(s) not converted — nothing written, because a PARTIAL conversion is the one outcome nobody can check $ echo $? 1 conflict, family and depends_on are refused on purpose rather than left for later: they state relationships between modules, which is a decision for the environment that replaces them, not something a converter can infer.
data.environments-and-hpc#Environments, and H:
A module system does two things: it resolves what a package needs, and it edits your shell. zpkgx +a +b already did the first. zpkge does the second — a front-end shaped like Lmod’s, over zpkgx’s own resolution, with no Lua interpreter and no modulefile tree.
It ships in the zpkgx binary; there is nothing else to install.
$ eval "$(zpkgs env init)" # in a profile $ zpkge load stedolan.github.io/jq $ command -v jq ~/.zpkg/stedolan.github.io/jq/v1.8.2/bin/jq $ zpkge list stedolan.github.io/jq $ zpkge unload stedolan.github.io/jq $ command -v jq /usr/bin/jq # back, exactly as it was zpkge save writes the current set to $ZPKG_DIR/collections/; zpkge restore purges and reloads it. zpkge purge unloads everything.
data.heterogeneous-clusters#A head node and c:
This is two failures at once, and the first one is invisible until it is not.
A store cannot hold two architectures. A prefix is $ZPKG_DIR//v/… — there is no platform anywhere in it. Measured on one machine, the same project and version staged twice:
…/openssl.org/v3.6.4/lib/libssl.so.3 ELF 64-bit x86-64 …/openssl.org/v3.6.4/lib/libssl.3.dylib Mach-O arm64 Those were kept apart only by being under two different ZPKG_DIRs. The file names differ there because the operating systems do — between linux/x86-64 and linux/aarch64 they are identical, lib/libssl.so.3 both times. A store shared over NFS holds whichever architecture was installed last, and the other one gets Exec format error from the kernel with nothing to explain it.
Give the platform a place in the path (bottle v0.60.0):
ZPKG_DIR=/shared/zpkgx/{platform} # one tree per architecture, one NFS export ZPKG_DIR=/shared/zpkgx/{os}/{arch} # the same, split {platform}, {os} and {arch} expand for the running machine, which is the point: the same exported string has to mean a different directory on each node. ⛔ Braces, not $ — the shell would expand $PLATFORM before zpkgx ever saw it, and a value the shell has already eaten cannot resolve per node. A path with no placeholder is used unchanged, so existing stores are untouched.
A store also records what it holds, in .zpkg-platform, so a shared tree read by the wrong architecture is refused with a sentence rather than by the kernel. A store written before that existed says nothing, and silence is read as agreement — the question closes the first time somebody installs into it.
And srun carries the head node’s PATH. Slurm’s --export defaults to ALL: “All of the user’s environment will be loaded from the caller’s environment.” So this is the wrong shape on a heterogeneous cluster —
zpkgx +hwloc +gnu.org/bash # resolves for the HEAD srun ./job.sh # …and that PATH lands on the node — because the PATH names the head’s binaries. Resolve on the node instead:
srun zpkgx +hwloc +gnu.org/bash -- ./job.sh zpkgx itself must then exist for the node’s architecture, at a path the node can reach. With {platform} in ZPKG_DIR, one export serves every node and each resolves its own tree.
data.named-environments#Named environments:
A site declares environments in HCL2 under $ZPKG_DIR/environments/:
# ~/.zpkg/environments/site.hcl2 env "cfd" { description = "the solver stack, as validated on 2026-09-01" packages = ["openmpi.org@5", "hdf5.org", "python.org@3.12"] } An env block takes description, packages, and the environment edits prepend_path, append_path, setenv and unsetenv.
$ zpkgs env avail cfd the solver stack, as validated on 2026-09-01 hdf5 HDF5 1.14.3 $ zpkgs env show cfd env "cfd" description the solver stack, as validated on 2026-09-01 declared in /home/you/.zpkg/environments/site.hcl2 package openmpi.org@5 package hdf5.org package python.org@3.12 $ zpkge load cfd An environment is not a lockfile: it names constraints, and the closure is resolved at load time from the signed registry, so a login node and a container agree.
data.two-things-no-code-here-removes#Two thin: MPI and the interconnect come from the host. libfabric/UCX, Slurm’s PMI and a vendor libmpi tied to a kernel driver cannot live in a hermetic tree. Bind-mount them, as Spack and Apptainer do. Metadata storms. Ten thousand ranks walking a shared $ZPKG_DIR will melt a Lustre MDS. Materialise once into a squashfs or SIF and mount it read-only. A read-only store is a deliberate arrangement, so nothing here ever fails because it could not write its platform marker into one.
data.why-unloading-is-exact#Why unloading is:
Loading never edits incrementally. It restores the environment it first saw and recomposes from the whole spec set, so unload b after load a b c leaves precisely what load a c would have — independent of the order things were loaded in.
The state that makes this work lives in the environment, not in the shell, and is read back by zpkgx:
PKGE_SPECS — the package set currently loaded. PKGE_BASE — the original value of every variable zpkgx has touched, base64 of NUL-separated NAME=value records. A variable’s base is captured once, the first time something touches it: the second load must not record the first load’s output as the pristine value. A variable that did not exist before is restored by being unset, not by being set empty — an empty PATH and no PATH are different to every program that reads one.
Lmod carries a module table for the same reason. This carries the base instead, which is smaller and cannot disagree with itself.
LOADEDMODULES is maintained, in Lmod’s own colon-separated spelling, because job scripts read it — if [[ $LOADEDMODULES == *openmpi* ]] is in thousands of them. _LMFILES_ is deliberately not set: it names modulefiles, there are none here, and an invented value is a lie a script could act on.
data.with-an-existing-lmod#With an existing L:
Generate modulefiles and let the site’s own Lmod load them. Nothing about module changes, and conflicts, hierarchies and spider keep working, because Lmod is still the one doing the work.
$ zpkgx --modulefile +openmpi.org@5 > $MODULEPATH_DIR/openmpi/5.0.8.lua zpkgx --json +... emits the same composed environment as data, for a tool that wants to compose it some other way.
data.without-one#Without one:
zpkgs env init --module also defines module and ml (load/add, unload/rm/del, purge, list, avail/av, show/display/whatis, save, restore, swap/switch) — for a container, a laptop, or a cluster built on this toolchain.
It refuses to install itself where an Lmod already exists:
zpkgx: an existing module system was found; not defining module(). zpkgx: publish modulefiles to MODULEPATH instead: zpkgx --modulefile +pkg Two implementations answering one command is how a support ticket becomes unanswerable, and the site’s own modulefiles are not ours to interpret.

data.cost#What this costs, and what we keep:
Dropped: four inherited decisions, each with the defect that made dropping it cheaper than keeping it — The break goes through them one at a time. The largest:
The shared store. go-zpkg installs into ~/.zpkg, not ~/.pkgx. Two reasons, and the second is the stronger: a hash in the path is not something pkgx can read, so the trees could not stay interchangeable anyway — and ~/.pkgx is pkgx’s directory, which upstream can be installed into on the same machine. Sharing it was the collision the rename existed to remove, left in the one place it does the most damage. Nothing is migrated: an existing ~/.pkgx is as much upstream’s as ours, and ZPKG_DIR=~/.pkgx keeps using it for anyone who wants that.
Kept: the pantry, the bottle format, the dependency grammar, the relocatable prefix, and the ability to resynchronise with upstream when recipes are added. Upstream’s recipes are converted to HCL2 rather than forked, so a periodic resync stays possible, and an improvement made here can be proposed back.
Not claimed: go-zpkg does not have Nix’s or Guix’s functional purity. But “not sandboxed” and “no time machine” are both vaguer than the code deserves, so here is what is actually there and what is actually missing.
data.filiation#Filiation:
go-zpkg descends from pkgx. It reads pkgx’s pantry, speaks pkgx’s bottle protocol, and resolves pkgx’s dependency ranges. Everything it installs is a pkgx package, and that is the point: the pantry is thousands of recipes that work, and nothing here would exist without them.
It is not a reimplementation of pkgx, and the difference is not a matter of ambition. Four things this needs are unreachable from pkgx’s design, not missing from its implementation, and all four are ordinary in Nix, Guix and Spack. This page says which, and what each one costs.
The honest summary: pkgx is excellent at one build of each version. Every difficulty below is a consequence of that one assumption, and it is an assumption an HPC site cannot make.
data.identity#3. An identity that is only a n:
Once a build is addressable, it needs to be identifiable: what makes this bottle this bottle. go-zpkg hashes a concrete spec — platform, declared variants, resolved closure, recipe plan digest, graft origin — in a length-prefixed canonical form, so no two different specs can serialise to the same bytes.
That is Spack’s answer, arrived at the same way. Spack’s hash was changed to include build, run and link dependencies and a canonical hash of the package.py file; the older hash had excluded build dependencies. The lesson it encodes — that the recipe is part of the identity, not merely its inputs — is one we took rather than relearned.
pkgx has no such object, and could not use one: with no variants and no place to put a second build, the identity of a package is its name and version.
data.isolation#The build is isolated, and her:
A factory build does not run on the host. builder/sovereign-build.sh enters unshare --mount --pid --fork and then chroots into a rootfs staged entirely from our own bottles — that is what “FROM scratch build” means here: neither the host’s libc nor the host’s compiler takes part, and the toolchain is a reviewed, committed list (builder/toolchain.txt, now also a members set in the pantry overlay) rather than whatever the distribution ships.
What that does not include, measured by searching for it rather than assuming: no network namespace, no user namespace, no seccomp profile. A build can reach the network. Nix’s sandbox denies it outright and admits only fixed-output derivations whose hash is declared in advance.
The gap is narrower than that sounds, because sources are pinned by content: an archive by digest, a git recipe by commit (bk’s source.go, fetch/fetch.go). What is missing is the enforcement — nothing stops a build step from fetching something nobody declared.
data.no-variants#1. A package specification w:
Upstream’s own corpus — docs.pkgx.sh/llms-full.txt, read 2026-11-04 — describes a grammar of a name and a version constraint, and nothing else:
node nodejs.org github.com/gabime/spdlog node^20.1.3 deno=1.35.3 "postgres>=12<14" +openssl # add to the environment Against that page: “The document describes no syntax for build options, variants, or feature flags. It describes no syntax for compiler selection.” In the C example, +clang is an ordinary +pkg addition — a package added to the environment, not a compiler chosen for a build.
Compare Spack, whose spec syntax is built around exactly this:
+debug # enable a boolean variant ~debug # disable it compression=gzip # single-valued fabrics=verbs,ofi # multi-valued: at LEAST these fabrics:=verbs,ofi # multi-valued: ONLY these and Guix, whose package transformation options do the same job from the other end — --with-input swaps a dependency through the whole graph, --with-c-toolchain rebuilds a package and its dependents with a different toolchain (the manual warns that this “minimizes incompatibility risks but cannot entirely eliminate them”, naming the C++ standard library and OpenMP runtimes), and --with-configure-flag appends to a package’s configure flags.
This is not decoration. +cuda, ~mpi, fabrics=verbs,ofi are the vocabulary an HPC site uses to say what it wants, and without them there is no way to ask for it.
go-zpkg adopts Spack’s spelling rather than inventing one, with one disambiguation forced by the filiation: ~ means two things. In pkgx it is a version range (~5.44 is >=5.44 <5.45); in Spack it disables a variant (~cuda). A digit after the tilde is a range, a letter is a variant.
data.one-build-per-version#2. A store path th:
The same upstream page states the layout plainly: ~/.pkgx//v/, with v*, v1 and v1.2 symlinks beside it. Deno 1.2.3 is at ~/.pkgx/deno.land/v1.2.3.
A path keyed on the version is a function of the version alone, so two builds of one version have one address. There is no bug to fix here; there is simply nowhere to put the second one. It is the direct consequence of §1 — with no way to ask for two builds, there was never a reason to store two.
Nix solves it with a digest in the path: a store path is a 20-byte digest in a custom Base32 (“20 arbitrary bytes become 32 ASCII characters”) followed by a hyphen and a readable name — /nix/store/b6gvzjyb2pg0kjfwrjmg1vfhh54ad73z-firefox-33.1 (store path specification).
Spack solves it with a DAG hash, computed from the JSON serialization of a concrete spec’s node dicts, and uses it “both to compare specs and to create unique installation directories for every possible configuration”. Its manual shows two mvapich2@2.2%gcc installations distinguished only by hash (qmt35td, er3die3), and /\ substitutes for a spec in any command.
go-zpkg extends the pkgx layout rather than replacing it:
//v3.3.11 identity not recorded //v3.3.11-habcdefghij012345 THIS build of 3.3.11 The bare form is kept and it is not a default. It is the honest statement that a bottle arrived without a spec annotation — mirrored, or built before the factory published one — and that nothing on disk can say which build it is. Minting a hash for it would put a claim in the path that no witness supports.
The hash is 16 characters of lowercase base32 because an OCI tag may contain [a-zA-Z0-9_][a-zA-Z0-9._-]{0,127} and not +, so Nix’s and Spack’s spellings of a spec cannot survive a round trip through a registry tag. The same suffix is used in the tag and in the directory name, from one constant, so the two cannot drift into two spellings of one idea.
data.time-machine#What a time machine would s:
bk lock is already most of the way, and it was written against Guix’s own statement of the problem — “to reproduce a profile bit-for-bit, manifests alone might not be enough”. It records the pantry revision, the overlay revision, every resolved version, a per-project spec hash over platform + version + parsed recipe + dependencies, and the version of bk that produced it.
It records more than a Guix manifest has to, and for a reason: a pkgx recipe’s versions: asks GitHub for tags at resolve time, so pinning the pantry revision is not enough. The same pantry commit resolved tcl to 9.0.4 and then to 9.1.0 four hours apart. The resolved version has to be written down or it is not pinned at all.
Four things stand between that and guix time machine:
The lock pins inputs, not output bytes. bk lock’s own documentation says so rather than implying otherwise: a bottle digest would pin them, and a lock taken before anything is built has no output to name. Nothing measures reproducibility. No build runs twice and compares. Until it does, “the same inputs give the same bottle” is a hope with no instrument behind it — and SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH is not set anywhere. The lock does not name the builder image it was built in, only the toolchain list that image is made from. Nothing re-executes the recorded bk. The version is written down; fetching that version and running it is still a human step. guix time machine does exactly this and it is the part that makes the rest usable. (1) and (3) are bookkeeping. (2) is the one that decides whether any of it is true, and it is the next thing to build.
data.verification#4. A distribution that cann:
pkgx’s dist.pkgx.dev serves tarballs over HTTPS. HTTPS authenticates the server, not the artifact: it says the bytes came from that host today, not that a particular build produced them.
go-zpkg publishes to an OCI registry with a Sigstore signature and an SLSA provenance statement per bottle, and verification is on by default — a bottle that cannot be verified is not installed, rather than installed with a warning. Mirrored bottles are distinguishable from built ones by their provenance: ours carries externalParameters and a versioned builder id, a mirror’s carries {} and an unversioned one.
Upstream remains reachable, as a choice rather than a default: ZPKG_DIST=https://dist.pkgx.dev with ZPKG_VERIFY=0, which is the honest pairing — unsigned distribution, verification off, said out loud.
data.visible#Where the filiation is visible i: bottle/pkgx.go pkgx’s version grammar, constraints and bottle protocol bottle/concrete.go the concrete spec and its hash — Spack’s idea bottle/storepath.go the store layout: pkgx’s, with a hash where there is one PantryBase upstream’s pantry, read directly ZPKG_DIST the distribution, defaulting to the signed registry

data.a-node-has-two-kinds-of-thing-under-it#A:
gnu.org has gnu.org/bash under it because of how it is named. curl.se has openssl.org under it because of what it needs.
The same words — “what is available under this node” — mean containment at a namespace and dependency at a package, and ls answers whichever the node is. Nix, Guix and Spack keep the two in separate commands (guix graph, nix-tree); here the node decides, because the person typing already knows which kind of thing they named.
A node can be both, and curl.se is. A trailing slash asks for the namespace — the only way to reach curl.se/ca-certs from curl.se — and a node that is both says where its other half is rather than hiding it.
$ zpkgs ls --tree curl.se curl.se — 8.17.0 curl.se/ca-certs nghttp2.org openssl.org curl.se/ca-certs (shown above) zlib.net --depth N bounds the descent. guix graph --max-depth exists for the same reason: the full transitive graph of anything interesting is pages long, and the first level is what a person reads. A diamond is expanded once and named once — and the one expanded is the direct dependency, because that is the one a reader came for.
It needs no network — not once zpkgs catalog update has run, and never again until you run it. zpkgx --graph answers the same question by resolving against the registry, which is the better answer when you have one and no answer at all in a FROM scratch image that has not fetched anything yet.
What it shows is what recipes declare. It is not the installed closure: bottle also pulls providers by soname that no recipe names, so a real install can hold more than this tree does.
data.a-platform-you-are-not-on#A platform you:
Both catalog update and --graph take --platform os/arch, because the answer is not the same everywhere and the question is usually asked from whichever machine you happen to be sitting at.
$ zpkgs catalog update --platform linux/x86-64 1915 project(s) → ~/.zpkg/catalog/linux-x86-64.json It writes to that platform’s own file, so ls and — which read the host’s — cannot mistake a foreign catalogue for yours.
And which platforms are there at all:
$ zpkgs catalog platforms darwin/aarch64 darwin/x86-64 linux/aarch64 linux/s390x linux/x86-64 windows/x86-64 ⛔ This exists because a list copied into a file froze while the registry grew. --platform could be guessed at one value at a time — an unpublished platform is refused with platform not in index, so the index plainly knows — and nothing could ask it for the set. The daily vulnerability scan carried its list in a workflow file, that list said two, and the registry published six at the time (seven now, which is the point); see Supply chain.
The output is an input: one platform per line and nothing else, ready to hand back to --platform from a loop. A failure is not an empty list — a loop that reads nothing and sees success scans nothing and calls it clean — so an unreadable index, a tag that is a single manifest, and an index naming no platform are each an error with its reason on stderr.
--graph answers the sharper question, the one a recipe author has:
$ zpkgx --graph +go.dev@^1.27.1 go.dev 1.27.1 └─ openssl.org 3.6.4 $ zpkgx --graph --platform linux/x86-64 +go.dev@^1.27.1 zpkgx: no version of go.dev satisfies "^1.27.1" AND is published for linux/x86-64 (available: 1.27.1 1.26.8 1.26.5 … (11 in all); satisfy but not published here: 1.27.1); asked for by ^1.27.1 (requested) “Satisfy but not published here” is the distinction that matters: the version exists as a tag and no bottle carries it for that platform. Before the flag, --graph resolved for the host and said so about everywhere.
⛔ ZPKG_CATALOG does not redirect --graph. ls, search and why read the file that variable names. --graph resolves against the registry and never opens it — so it refuses rather than answering about the wrong machine:
$ ZPKG_CATALOG=~/.zpkg/catalog/linux-x86-64.json zpkgx --graph +go.dev zpkgx: ZPKG_CATALOG names …/linux-x86-64.json, and --graph does not read a catalogue — it resolves against the registry. To ask about another platform: --graph --platform os/arch It used to answer the host’s resolution there, with exit 0 and no sign the file was never opened (go-zpkg/zpkgx#110). A catalogue records what is published; --graph resolves what would satisfy a constraint, including versions no bottle carries. Those are different questions, and the “satisfy but not published here” line above depends on telling them apart.
The price is that the index goes stale and nothing tells you by magic, so every command that reads it says how old it is:
$ zpkgs catalog /home/you/.zpkg/catalog/linux-x86-64.json 1908 project(s), 986 with dependencies, 2 hour(s) old
data.and-it-remembers#And it remembers:
The hint fires once, in front of somebody who is in the middle of something else. zpkgs request answers about one project at the moment you ask it. Neither can tell you that the same package has failed eleven times this month, which is the thing worth acting on:
$ zpkgs journal 2 failure(s) recorded here, 1 of them a package this registry does not have most asked for and not here: 1 aerc-mail.org `zpkgs request ` turns one of those into a report you can open as an issue. It sends nothing, and neither does this. It is a local file, and that is the whole design. The useful signal from a package manager is which packages people reach for and do not get, and the usual way to collect it is to phone home. This does not: it keeps the promise request already makes a few paragraphs above, and adds the only thing request cannot — memory. ZPKG_JOURNAL=0 records nothing at all, and zpkgs journal --clear removes it.
A record of failures is still a thing that can go wrong, so three properties are tested rather than intended:
it cannot fail the command it records a store that cannot be written is a reason for the journal to stay empty, not for zpkgx node to fail it cannot grow without bound a failing command in a loop would otherwise fill the disk — one rotation, capped it cannot carry what it cannot print the text is an error string quoting names read out of a catalogue, a registry index or a downloaded binary, so it is sanitised on the way in A fourth came from the test rather than the design: a crash mid-write leaves a line with no newline, and appending onto it glued the next entry to the damaged one — one interrupted write costing two records.
data.and-what-any-of-it-is-for#And what any o:
A size is not a decision. --root says what a lock needs:
$ zpkgs store --root seed.lock.hcl … 41.2 GiB over 363 version(s) of 302 project(s) against 1 root(s): 12.3 MiB live over 7 version(s), 41.2 GiB in 356 version(s) no root needs dead here means NOT REACHABLE FROM THE ROOTS YOU NAMED, and nothing is removed guix gc draws the line this copies: “any file under /gnu/store reachable from a root is considered live and cannot be deleted; any other file is considered dead”. What makes that safe is that the roots are explicit — guix keeps them as symlinks under /var/guix/gcroots, and --list-live reports before gc removes.
A lock is already a root set. zpkgx --lock pins every project in the closure, not only what you typed, so membership in it is reachability — no graph walk and no network. An environment would not do: it names constraints, which have to be resolved against the registry, and this command works offline.
Three things worth knowing:
the version counts, not just the project: llvm 16.0.6 is dead while 22.1.8 is live; several --root flags union, because that is what reachable from any of them means; without --root there is no live/dead line at all — “nothing is reachable from nothing” is true and would read as a verdict on your disk. A mistyped --root is refused before the store is walked: eight seconds over 41 GiB is too long to wait to be told the arguments were wrong.
data.and-what-that-has-cost-you#And what that:
A ✓ is per project. zpkgs store is the whole disk:
$ zpkgs store --by-size -n 6 ~/.zpkg llvm.org 13.8 GiB 3 versions, 8.5 GiB not the newest here android.com/cmdline-tools 6.4 GiB swift.org 4.6 GiB github.com/coqui-ai/TTS 1.6 GiB go.dev 1.5 GiB 7 versions, 1.3 GiB not the newest here gohugo.io 1020.5 MiB 13 versions, 934.6 MiB not the newest here … 296 more 41.2 GiB over 363 version(s) of 302 project(s) 12.8 GiB is in versions that are not the newest present — which is not the same as unused Every ephemeral run leaves its bottles behind and nothing removes one. zpkgm list answers a different question — what you asked to have installed — so a bottle pulled six months ago to run one command is in neither. Those figures are one developer’s machine on 2026-10-08, and thirteen versions of gohugo.io is not a number anybody chose.
data.completion#Completion:
eval "$(zpkgs completion bash)" # or zsh, or: zpkgs completion fish | source $ zpkgx +gnu.org/ba +gnu.org/bash $ zpkgx gnu.o gnu.org/ # with the slash, so the next TAB descends The snippet is a few lines and does nothing but call zpkgx. Spack generates spack-completion.bash from its command tree and commits it; Guix hand-writes one per shell; both then need a check that the file still matches the program. Nix took the other road — the binary answers when NIX_GET_COMPLETIONS names the argument being completed — and that is the one followed here.
The reason is specific: what is being completed is not a fixed command tree, it is the registry, which changes without zpkgx changing and which a generated file could never be level with. It is also the only shape that works in a FROM scratch image, where there is no completion framework, no python and no generator to run.
data.everything-is-named-what-is-here-is-mark:
$ zpkgs ls doxygen.nl doxygen.nl — no bottle here $ zpkgs ls --tree curl.se curl.se — 8.17.0 curl.se/ca-certs 2026.09.25 doxygen.nl (no bottle here) openssl.org 3.6.0 A catalogue is published per platform, because what is available differs by architecture — the s390x lane has a fraction of what linux/x86-64 has.
Dropping the name would tell you the project does not exist, which is false. Printing it bare tells you nothing. Marking it tells you it exists, that there is no bottle for you, and therefore that building it is the thing to do next.
In a tree, that mark is usually the most useful line on the page: an unsatisfiable dependency is the reason the thing above it cannot be installed, and it would otherwise print as a bare name among satisfied ones. It reaches too, as the description beside the candidate — the moment it is worth knowing, before the name is typed rather than after it fails.
What is behind the mark: the factory asks the registry, per project, which versions it carries and whether this platform is among them. Two things it deliberately does not do. It does not borrow: a version list that fell back to the upstream dist.pkgx.dev is dropped, because “available” is a claim about one registry and a list from another one answers a different question. And it does not assume: a tag listing spans every architecture, so a mirror wave that lands x86-64 publishes a tag s390x cannot use, and the version recorded is the newest this platform really carries.
data.finding-packages#Finding packages:
A package manager you cannot browse is a package manager you have to already know. zpkgs ls walks the tree; completes into it.
$ zpkgs catalog update 1908 project(s) → /home/you/.zpkg/catalog/linux-x86-64.json $ zpkgs ls curl.se 8.17.0, 3 under github.com 452 under gnu.org 54 under zlib.net 1.3.2 $ zpkgs ls gnu.org gnu.org/autoconf 2.73 gnu.org/bash 5.3 gnu.org/gcc 16.2.0, 1 under … $ zpkgs ls curl.se curl.se — 8.17.0 curl.se/ca-certs nghttp2.org openssl.org zlib.net also a namespace, 3 under it: zpkgs ls curl.se/
data.how-many-are-marked-and-how-to-ask#How m:
The mark is not rare. Measured against the published darwin/aarch64 catalogue on 2026-10-23, 567 of 1940 projects have a recipe and no bottle — 29% of the pantry. zpkgs ls marks each one as you meet it; to see them as a list rather than one at a time:
$ go run ./internal/catstat -missing ~/.zpkg/catalog/darwin-aarch64.json 567 of 1940 project(s) have no bottle here aerc-mail.org agpt.co … A percentage is not a work list: nobody can file, build or triage 29%.
When you want one of them, zpkgs request turns “this is missing” into a report somebody can act on — and sends nothing:
$ zpkgs request aerc-mail.org project aerc-mail.org platform darwin/aarch64 zpkgs 0.26.0 state published for linux/aarch64, NOT for darwin/aarch64 Nothing was sent. `zpkgs request --url aerc-mail.org` prints a link that opens this as an issue. --url prints a prefilled issue link you read first. There is no flag that posts and nothing to configure or forget: the only way a report reaches GitHub is a person clicking a link they have already seen in full.
The payload is a fixed list — project, platform, tool version, state — assembled by a function that does not import os, so it cannot reach argv or the environment even by accident. That is deliberate. The command that prompted all of this was
$ zpkgx openstack user list --domain stratuslab and a reporter that attached “the command that failed” would have published an organisation’s infrastructure names into a public tracker, from a machine whose owner was debugging rather than publishing.
A request for something already here is refused rather than filed: an issue whose premise is false spends a maintainer’s trust.
data.it-reports-and-deletes-nothing#It report:
That is deliberate, and it is the same line every comparable tool draws: nix path-info -S against nix store gc, guix gc --list-live against guix gc, spack find against spack gc. All three make the roots explicit before removing anything.
There is no profile here, so there is no root set: a version that looks superseded may be exactly what a lock pins or what an environment asks for. So the last line states a fact about the disk and says in as many words that it is not the same as unused.
data.one-command-fetches-it#One command fetch:
zpkgs catalog update is the only thing on the read path that asks the registry what exists — catalog platforms below asks it too, and is the one other command that does. ls, search, why, browse and read the file update wrote, and nothing on that path opens a socket.
That line is the difference between a completion you leave switched on and one you turn off. A is a fresh process — there is no state between two presses — so a fetch on the read path is paid again on every press, in full. Measured, one press of on gnu.o:
median answer fetching on every press 295 ms nothing reading the file 7.6 ms gnu.org/ guix pull and nix-channel --update put the line in the same place.
data.running-exactly-what-a-lock-pins#Running:
$ zpkgx --lock seed.lock.hcl -- make zpkgx: seed.lock.hcl, 231 pin(s), 3 hour(s) old A lock nobody consumes is a record, not a mechanism: cargo’s --locked and npm’s ci exist because the file only means something once a command refuses to deviate from it.
The defect is not hypothetical here. The same pantry commit resolved tcl to 9.0.4 and then to 9.1.0 four hours apart, because a recipe’s versions: asks GitHub at resolution time.
Every pin becomes a root, not just the lock’s own — that is what makes it a lock rather than a hint, and a set that cannot be satisfied exactly fails instead of materialising something near it. A lock taken on another platform is refused by name: 537 of 1908 projects available on linux/x86-64 have no bottle for darwin/aarch64.
An environment is still not a lockfile. An environment names a set and resolves it afresh; a lock names versions. Two paths, side by side.
data.shipping-a-catalogue-with-the-image#Ship:
ZPKG_CATALOG= reads one from somewhere else entirely — for an air-gapped image, or to inspect a catalogue before publishing it. An image that ships one can also simply drop the file at the path zpkgs catalog prints, and never fetch at all.
Set and unreadable is a refusal, not a quiet fall back to the local store: somebody who names a file means that file, and answering from somewhere else under a header blaming the registry would be three wrong things in one line.
data.the-failure-says-where-to-go#The failure:
That only helps somebody who knows the command exists, so the failure itself names it:
$ zpkgx +aerc-mail.org -- echo ok zpkgx: no version of aerc-mail.org is published for darwin/aarch64 (available: 0.22.0; not published here: 0.22.0) zpkgx: if it should be here: `zpkgs request aerc-mail.org` prints a report you can open as an issue (it sends nothing) The hint fires on a type, not on words in a message. An earlier version matched the text and turned up on
zpkgx: command not found in the requested packages: true where the package was published and the command was missing — and a hint that appears on unrelated failures teaches people to ignore hints. A build that failed, a signature that did not verify and a registry having a bad day get none: none of them is something to ask a maintainer to publish.
data.the-two-questions-that-do-not-descend#Th:
Everything above descends. ls --tree says what a project needs, which is what you ask before installing it. Two questions point the other way, and no amount of descending reaches them.
Who needs this — what you ask before changing something:
$ zpkgs ls --dependents openssl.org openssl.org — 4.0.2 ✓ 3.6.0 agwa.name/git-crypt (no bottle here) apache.org/arrow 25.0.1 … runtime dependents on darwin/aarch64; a build-only user is in no catalogue The number is the point — it is the blast radius of a bump, and before this it could not be obtained at all. Counted on the catalogues published 2026-10-06, and it is not one number:
platform need openssl directly transitively (--tree) darwin/aarch64 153 789 linux/aarch64 164 854 Out of 1908 projects in each. The two differ because a catalogue records what a platform really carries, so a project with no bottle here has no edges here. That is why the command prints the platform under the list rather than leaving the figure to be quoted bare.
Why is this in here — what you ask when a closure holds a surprise:
$ zpkgs why git-scm.org zlib.net git-scm.org — 2.55.0 ✓ 2.47.1 → zlib.net — 1.3.2 ✓ A shortest path, as nix why-depends answers it: the point is an explanation a person can hold, not every route. When there is none it says so and exits 1, which is the answer that tells you a bump cannot reach you.
Every comparable tool has the first question and they do not all mean the same thing by it. spack dependents is direct, or transitive with -t. guix refresh --list-dependent is about what would need rebuilding, and its manual says plainly that it only approximates that.
data.two-things-about-the-figures#Two things:
It walks the tree, so it costs seconds rather than milliseconds — eight over 41 GiB. That is why it is its own command and not a line in zpkgx catalog: nothing on the path may cost that.
Sizes are powers of 1024 and say so with the i. du counts blocks and this counts file sizes, so the two disagree twice over; naming the unit is the least a report can do about that.
data.walking-it-full-screen#Walking it full-s:
$ zpkgs browse gnu.org — 54 > gnu.org/bash 5.3 ✓ gnu.org/gcc no bottle here +gnu.org/make 4.4.1 ↑ ↓ move · → descend · ← back · tab names ⇄ dependencies · / search · space pin · q quit, printing what is pinned nix-tree is the precedent: the same data read one node at a time is data nobody explores. Descending into a leaf shows what it needs, rather than making you press tab.
q prints what you pinned on stdout while the screen goes to stderr, so zpkgx +$(zpkgs browse) composes. It reads the cached catalogue and nothing else — 0.013 s against the real 1908-project one — and without a terminal it prints the tree and exits, because zpkgs browse | less, a CI log and a scratch image are the same case.
data.what-this-answer-is-not#What this answer:
The catalogue carries runtime dependencies, reduced for one platform. So --dependents is the runtime blast radius on the platform you are standing on: who would load different bytes if this project changed.
It is not the rebuild set. A build dependency is paid once by the factory and is in nobody’s installed closure, so it is not in a catalogue and cannot be in this answer. Guix is about rebuilds and says it approximates them; this is about closures and is exact for what it covers. The line is printed under the list, not only written here, because a number is read where it is printed.
And why answers from the declared graph. Nix answers from the store, by scanning built output for the hash parts of store paths — there is nothing to scan before anything is installed, and saying which it is beats implying a scan nobody ran.
data.what-you-already-have#What you already h:
$ zpkgs ls --tree curl.se curl.se — 8.17.0 ✓ curl.se/ca-certs 2026.09.25 ✓ doxygen.nl (no bottle here) openssl.org 3.6.0 ✓ 3.5.1 A catalogue says what exists; a reader standing in front of it mostly wants to know what they have. nix and guix show the state of the store in everything they print.
A bare ✓ when what is installed is the version on offer, and ✓ when it is not — the case worth the extra word, because it is the one where a command would fetch something new.
data.when-there-is-none#When there is none:
zpkgs ls falls back to what is installed, and says so in its header — with the sentence that fits the case it is actually in:
$ zpkgs ls # never fetched one zpkgs: showing what is INSTALLED — no catalogue yet; run: zpkgs catalog update $ zpkgs ls # one is there and will not parse zpkgs: showing what is INSTALLED — /home/you/.zpkg/catalog/linux-x86-64.json could not be read Those two are not the same state, and “run zpkgs catalog update” is the fix for the first and no help at all for the second. Sending somebody to a command that cannot work is worse than saying nothing.
Offline, and in a fresh scratch image before the first fetch, the fallback is not a lesser answer: it is the only true one available, and it is often the one wanted, because completing onto something already installed costs nothing to run.
The two lists are never merged. “Available” about a mix of a registry and a local store is a word with no meaning, and a header cannot be honest about a list with two sources.
data.where-the-list-comes-from#Where the list:
gnu.org/ has to know what exists, and a registry cannot be asked:
GET /v2/_catalog 403 (ghcr issues no token) GET /v2/go-zpkg/packages/zlib.net/tags/list 200 ["1.3.2", …] Versions, yes. Projects, no.
Nix, Guix and Spack all answer this from a local index — an eval cache, a channel checkout, a package repo. The zpkgx-native equivalent is an artefact in the registry itself, so the registry carries a catalogue:
$ bk catalog --pantry … --overlay … -o catalog.json catalog: 1908 project(s) → catalog.json 1908 projects, 905 roots, 100 KB, built in 0.4 s with no network. It is an ordinary bottle — signed, attested, mirrored and cached like any other, fetched in one pull — and it is published per platform, because what is available differs by architecture and a single list would tell most readers that packages are available which, for them, are not.
Seven lanes publish one each. Do not read the list from here — this sentence has already been wrong once, when the seventh lane was added and nothing in this file knew. Ask the registry, which is the only thing that knows:
$ zpkgs catalog platforms darwin/aarch64 darwin/x86-64 linux/aarch64 linux/s390x linux/x86-64 wasip1/wasm windows/x86-64 A platform with no catalogue would give you silence, which is not the same answer as “nothing is available here”. wasip1/wasm is the odd one and has its own page: its modules are statically linked, so a catalogue entry there names build-time dependencies that are not themselves published for that platform.
Signed, and checked: forging a catalogue does not get an unsigned bottle installed, because the install path verifies anyway. It gets a near-miss name offered at your prompt, which is the whole of a typosquat. The attack is on the reader.
data.you-know-the-command-not-the-package#You:
$ zpkgs search rg crates.io/ripgrep rg 14.1.1 aardvark.io/rgbds rgbasm 0.9.0 rg is crates.io/ripgrep. No guess at the project name reaches it, and — a prefix on the project path — never will either. Completion and search are different tools, and that is the line between them.
nix search, guix search and spack list -s all match a package’s description, which is right for a collection that has descriptions. This pantry does not. Counted on the catalogue published for linux/aarch64 on 2026-10-06: of its 1908 projects, 1582 name the commands they put on PATH and six carry a summary. A search over prose would find six packages.
Those figures are not a recollection: go run ./internal/catstat ~/.zpkg/catalog/*.json in go-zpkg/zpkgx prints them from the file you have, through the same parser the client uses, so you can check them against your own catalogue rather than against this page. Both published platforms agree on the number that matters — six — and differ where you would expect them to, 1430 projects with a bottle on linux/aarch64 against 1371 on darwin/aarch64.
So the match is on names and on commands, ranked by how a thing matched rather than by how often — a command named exactly what you typed is what you meant, every time. Nothing found exits non-zero, so zpkgs search x || echo none works.

data.dlfail-package-fetch-failure-resolving-t:

data.fix-applied-soname-exact-closure-complet:
Re-running the 81 MISSING + DLFAIL projects after the fix, 73 now run FROM scratch (25 exit 0, 48 launch their closure and return non-zero/timeout on --version — not failures). All 40 DLFAIL are resolved; MISSING drops from 41 to 8.
Root cause: the closure completer mapped an unsatisfied soname to its provider project and pulled that project’s latest package — but a soname carries an ABI version a newer release may have moved past (a binary needs libxml2.so.2, yet libxml2 2.15 ships libxml2.so.16; libssl.so.1.1 is openssl 1.1.x while the latest is 3.x). The provider was often already present as a declared dep at the wrong version, so completion skipped it. The fix walks the provider’s versions and installs the newest that ships the exact soname (prioritising versions whose leading number matches the soname’s ABI tail, so libssl.so.1.1 finds openssl 1.1.1w directly); the drifted and latest packages coexist on LD_LIBRARY_PATH. Ten soname mappings were also added (libFLAC, libtheora, libgit2, libcbor, libavro, libprotoc, libclang, libtinfow, libgflags, and the libboost prefix).

data.interpretation#Interpretation:
NOBIN, OTHER:1 and OTHER:124 are not FROM-scratch failures. NOBIN projects are libraries with no runnable binary (an artifact of probing every project with run … --version); OTHER:1 binaries launched their closure and merely lack a --version flag; OTHER:124 binaries ran but blocked because --version dropped them into a REPL, server loop, or stdin wait. In all three the loader resolved PT_INTERP, the closure assembled, and the ELF executed — which is exactly what “runs FROM scratch” tests. Counting them as failures would understate conformance.
The 4.7% of real gaps are concentrated, not random. The MISSING and DLFAIL rows are dominated by large C/C++ applications with big plugin closures — gtk3/gtk4, php, ruby, imagemagick, mpv, httpd, libvips, librsvg, and similar. Those programs assemble much of their runtime graph through dlopen at runtime (image codecs, format plugins, language modules) rather than through DT_NEEDED at link time. A static closure completed from DT_NEEDED cannot see edges that only exist when the program dlopens a plugin by name during execution, so zpkgm neither pulls those packages nor knows the soname to map. This is a known, structural limitation of DT_NEEDED-derived closures, and it is the single largest source of the remaining gaps. A second, smaller source is version-pin drift — packages built against a soname (libssl.so.1.1, the abseil …so.2401/2501 variants) that no currently-published package provides; zpkgx itself would fail those too. libudev.so.1 and librt.so.1 are a third, minor source: system sonames the zpkgx package set does not ship standalone.
This does not change the earlier conclusion; it quantifies it. The DT_NEEDED-driven closure resolves the implicit graph for the large majority of the pantry, and the residual gaps are honest, understood, and — for MISSING and DLFAIL — actionable through soname→project mappings or upstream package fixes.

data.pantry-wide-audit#Pantry-wide audit:
An audit of the whole pantry (linux/aarch64):
Availability — 1818 of 1896 projects (96%) publish a linux package, so nearly the entire pantry is a FROM-scratch candidate. Runtime sample — a diverse 100-project sample run under zpkgm run … --version: 39 PASS, 38 no runnable bin / no --version (libraries; harness bias), 20 non-zero exit on --version (mostly tools without a --version flag), and only 2 missing-library failures — both libabsl_* (abseil), in grpc.io (grpc_csharp_plugin) and mosh.org. This is a pantry package-vs-declared-dependency drift; zpkgx itself would fail there too. No consumer tool can supply a soname no package ships.
Net: the DT_NEEDED-driven closure resolves the implicit graph across the pantry, with the only observed failures being upstream version-pin drift. The soname → project table also gained prefix matching (projectForSoname) for multi-.so projects such as abseil (libabsl_*), protobuf and re2.
data.proposal-to-the-pkgx-pantry-maintainers#:
The information needed to run a package standalone (its complete runtime closure) exists at build time but is not published. Two complementary asks:
Publish the resolved runtime closure per package — e.g. a deps.json next to versions.txt on dist.pkgx.dev, listing the transitive project@version set actually linked (including the implicit libc/gcc/libz/… that package.yml omits). This lets any tool assemble a complete, relocatable environment without re-deriving it from DT_NEEDED.
Optionally, an explicit platforms/runtime declaration for the implicit system libraries a package links, so FROM scratch consumers are first-class.
go-zpkg/zpkgm is a working proof of concept: a single pure-Go, CGO_ENABLED=0 binary that resolves the closure from DT_NEEDED and runs real packages (bash, curl, node, python, perl, …) on a FROM scratch image with zero system dependencies. See https://github.com/go-zpkg/zpkgm.

data.what-zpkgm-does#What zpkgm does:
zpkgm run (and zpkgm install --from-scratch) iterate to a fixpoint: scan the installed packages’ ELF DT_NEEDED (via Go’s debug/elf) and, for every soname not yet provided by the closure, pull the package that provides it:
glibc set (libc, libm, libpthread, libdl, librt, …) → gnu.org/glibc libgcc_s, libstdc++ → gnu.org/gcc/libstdcxx libatomic, libgomp → gnu.org/gcc common undeclared libraries → a curated soname → project table (see sonameProject in closure.go): libz, libbz2, liblzma, libzstd, liblz4, ncurses/libtinfo, readline, libffi, pcre2, gettext, libiconv, libidn2, libunistring, libpsl, nghttp2, expat, libxml2, sqlite3, gmp, mpfr, libcrypt → libxcrypt, … Wrapper scripts (#!/bin/sh, e.g. git) are run under the **zpkgx gnu.org/bash
gnu.org/coreutils**, which zpkgm installs and points /bin/sh at — zpkgm is a package manager, so it uses the real zpkgx shell rather than reimplementing one. (An earlier attempt embedded a pure-Go shell, but its set -e semantics diverged from dash/bash and broke git’s wrapper; real bash behaves correctly.)
data.why-packages-dont-just-run-on-scratch#Wh:
A zpkgx package assumes a host system. Two structural gaps surface on scratch:
The interpreter path. Every dynamic ELF has PT_INTERP=/lib/ld-linux-* — an absolute system path that does not exist on a scratch image. zpkgm run symlinks the pkgx glibc loader to /lib/ld-linux-* (and /bin/sh to itself) so parent and child ELFs resolve natively.
Incomplete runtime dependency graphs. A package’s package.yml dependencies: is not its full runtime closure. Examples measured:
package links (DT_NEEDED) declares in package.yml gnu.org/wget libz only openssl.org curl.se libz, libzstd, libnghttp2 (transitive only) perl.org libcrypt (libxcrypt) — zpkgx compensates with build-time-detected metadata that is not exposed on dist.pkgx.dev (no deps.json; all such URLs 404). So zpkgm rebuilds the closure from the packages’ own DT_NEEDED — see below.

data.a-bottle-that-runs-somewhere-else#A bott:
$ZPKG_DIR is wherever you put it. A package that records where it was built is not a package, it is a souvenir — so every binary is normalised before it is signed, and the two platforms need different work.
Linux. A DT_RUNPATH naming the build machine is rewritten $ORIGIN-relative, so a library found beside the binary is found beside it anywhere. The entry can be rewritten in place, because the replacement is shorter than what it replaces.
macOS. Two things have to be right at once, and each fails silently on its own.
A Mach-O names its dependencies by the install name the dependency was built with. Two forms of that name cannot work here:
install name why it fails /Users/runner/.pkgx/…/libssh2.1.dylib absolute — an absolute reference never consults an rpath, so no rpath rescues it @rpath/libzstd.1.dylib bare — a consumer’s rpath reaches $ZPKG_DIR, not the library’s own lib/, so it resolves nowhere The second is CMake’s default (MACOSX_RPATH) and is the more insidious of the two: the package that carries it works perfectly, because its own binaries reach its libraries through @loader_path/../lib. Only other packages break.
Both are normalised to @rpath//v/lib/, with a dependency’s version reduced to its major so that a dependency’s minor upgrade does not orphan its dependents.
And the binary must carry an rpath that actually reaches $ZPKG_DIR from where it installs. That one is linked in at build time rather than repaired afterwards: its value is how deep the package installs, which is a fact about the recipe and cannot be recovered from the binary. A bottle whose references to other packages resolve only through the builder’s own absolute rpath is refused, not published.
Every Mach-O the factory edits is re-signed. On Apple silicon a binary whose signature describes the old bytes is not stale — it is killed on sight, with no message.
data.consuming#Consuming:
Point the go-zpkg tools at the registry and verify against the pinned key:
ZPKG_DIST=oci://ghcr.io/go-pkgx/packages ZPKG_VERIFY=1 zpkgm install lz4.org ZPKG_VERIFY=1 is fail-closed: an unsigned or badly-signed package is refused, not installed. See supply chain for the verification model.
Or consume the same packages from the GitHub Pages zpkgx-dist mirror:
ZPKG_DIST=https://go-zpkg.github.io/packages zpkgm install lz4.org Packages are OCI artifacts, so any OCI client can also pull them directly:
docker pull ghcr.io/go-pkgx/packages/lz4.org:1.10.0
data.except-what-was-mirrored#Except what was:
Not every package here was built here. Where a bottle already exists upstream and rebuilding it would buy nothing, the factory copies it and republishes it with our own signature, SBOM and provenance. Those attestations are ours and mean what they say: this is the artefact we published, and this is where it came from.
What they do not mean is that the normalisation above was applied. A mirrored bottle is republished byte-for-byte; nothing unpacks it, so nothing rewrites its install names and no guard refuses it. It carries whatever the upstream build produced — including, in at least one published case, a RUNPATH naming absolute paths under /opt that exist on nobody’s machine.
You can tell which is which by looking:
linux DT_RUNPATH macOS LC_RPATH built here $ORIGIN-relative several @loader_path/.. depths and the builder’s absolute path mirrored whatever upstream wrote one @loader_path entry, or an absolute path
data.package-registry#Package registry: ghcr.io/go-pkgx/packages is a pure-Go package factory: it builds zpkgx pantry recipes and publishes signed, attested packages for every platform through two channels.
data.the-factory#The factory:
The go-zpkg/packages repo is the factory. GitHub Actions workflows build each recipe with bk — the CGO-free re-implementation of brewkit — and publish the result to both channels.
Factories: build.yml (linux), darwin.yml (macOS), windows.yml (Go) + windows-rust.yml (Rust) + windows-proof.yml (e2e), each publishing to the OCI registry and uploading a zpkgx dist tree; a single pages.yml aggregator unions the latest run of every build into the combined Pages mirror. wasip1/wasm (pilot): wasip1.yml cross-builds pure-Go projects with GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm CGO_ENABLED=0, runs each module under wasmtime, then publishes it to the OCI registry only (no Pages mirror yet) with the OCI platform os=wasip1, architecture=wasm (zpkgx slug wasip1/wasm). The module is bin/.wasm; a recipe’s provides: bin/ stays extension-free and bottle.ResolveBinPath finds the .wasm, as it finds .exe on Windows. Pilots: filippo.io/age 1.3.2, github.com/cpuguy83/go-md2man 2.0.7, mvdan.cc/sh (shfmt) 3.14.1. The build side is bk’s wasip1/wasm target (BREWKIT_TARGET=wasip1/wasm, triple wasm32-wasip1; wasm is an architecture of wasip1 only). wasip1/wasm C tools: wasip1-c.yml builds C with our own toolchain, not a prebuilt wasi-sdk: the llvm.org bottle (clang, wasm-ld, llvm-ar) plus two cross parts built from source in the pantry overlay, following wasi-sdk’s cmake/wasi-sdk-sysroot.cmake — compiler-rt.llvm.org/wasi (builtins for wasm32-wasip1 and clang’s headers, as a clang resource dir) and github.com/WebAssembly/wasi-libc (the sysroot). bk --platform wasip1/wasm build adds the three bottles and imposes clang --target=wasm32-wasip1 --sysroot=… -resource-dir=… -mcpu=lime1 --rtlib=compiler-rt through $BK_CC / $BK_CXX, the stencil the cc/gcc/clang shims re-exec. Published as wasip1/wasm after a run under wasmtime: zlib.net 1.3.2 (libz.a, minigzip), sqlite.org 3.53.4 (the shell) and lua.org 5.4.9 (errors via setjmp/longjmp, compiled to the standard WebAssembly exception-handling instructions — a pcall(error) runs under wasmtime 50). The build runs inside the sovereign rootfs (bk builder’s tree, entered by builder/sovereign-bk.sh), so sh, make, coreutils, clang and wasm-ld are bottles in that tree and a “what ran, from where” step prints their resolved paths from inside the chroot; the runner contributes three static Go binaries, the namespace and wasmtime. C++: a third source-built bottle, libcxx.llvm.org/wasi (libc++ and libc++abi, no exceptions, from wasi-sdk’s define_libcxx_sub), named by the $BK_CXX stencil when installed; pilot github.com/simdjson/simdjson 5.0.5 (upstream’s library plus a small minifier driver), run under wasmtime. Pilots and toolchain bottles are published for linux/aarch64 hosts too (native ubuntu-24.04-arm runner). Not yet: C++ exceptions (wasi-sdk’s DUAL flavour, -fwasm-exceptions plus libunwind) and darwin hosts. Schedule: each factory runs on a schedule (plus manual workflow_dispatch). Auth: the workflow’s native GITHUB_TOKEN (permissions.packages: write) — no long-lived PAT to manage or rotate. Ordering: requested projects are expanded to their topologically-ordered runtime-dependency closure, so every dependency is built before its dependents. Idempotent: any (project, version, platform) already in ghcr is skipped, so shared dependencies build once and the catalog grows progressively. Per-recipe failures are logged, never fatal; the recipe list is grown outward from dependency-free leaves toward the full pantry.

Most of the catalog is a zpkgx pantry recipe built here. These are projects upstream does not carry at all — the HPC and GPU floor an MPI actually needs, which the pantry stops just above:

data.two-channels-every-platform#Two channels:
Every platform — linux/x86-64, linux/aarch64, darwin/aarch64, darwin/x86-64 and windows/x86-64 — publishes to both:
the signed OCI registry ghcr.io/go-pkgx/packages (each package carrying an SBOM, provenance and signature as OCI referrers), and a GitHub Pages zpkgx-dist mirror at https://go-zpkg.github.io/packages, carrying all platforms side by side (///…).
data.upstream-zpkgx-cannot-read-it#⛔ Upstream:
libpkgx’s SemVer constructor (src/utils/semver.ts:26-41, read 2026-11-02) splits a version on . and accepts a part only if it matches /^(\d+)([a-z])$/ — last part only — or /^\d+$/; anything else throws invalid version. 3.3.11_1 has the part 11_1, which matches neither.
Pointing an upstream zpkgx client at this registry is therefore unsupported once a project carries a rebuild. That was weighed rather than overlooked: it throws rather than resolving the wrong bottle, which is the better of the two failures. zpkgx, zpkgs and zpkgm from this org read _N correctly.
The alternatives were rejected for reasons worth knowing if you are tempted by them. A fourth numeric component (3.3.11.1) parses upstream but cannot be told apart from a genuine four-component release such as ghc 5.64.3.2. A letter suffix (3.3.11a) parses upstream but caps at 26 and occupies the slot real versions use — openssl ships 1.1.1w. Build metadata (3.3.11+neon) cannot be a tag at all: the OCI distribution spec requires [a-zA-Z0-9_][a-zA-Z0-9._-]{0,127}, and semver itself says build metadata “MUST be ignored when determining version precedence”, so it could not express supersedes even if it fitted.

Packages are ordinary OCI artifacts — each with a signature, an SBOM, and a provenance statement attached as referrers.
