data.when-one-version-has-two-builds#When one:
A recipe fix can change the binary without changing the upstream version. Measured on 2026-11-02: fftw.org gained its SIMD codelets, was rebuilt, and published as 3.3.11 — the tag the scalar build already had. nm on the two shows 0 → 207 _neon symbols in both the single- and double-precision libraries. Plainly different bottles, and nothing in the registry said so; anyone holding the old one kept it, because the version they had and the version on offer were the same string.
So a version may carry a trailing _N rebuild counter — 3.3.11_1 is the same upstream sources built again. It is Homebrew’s rebuild and Debian’s +bN, and it behaves the way those do:
3.3.11 < 3.3.11_1 < 3.3.11_2 < 3.3.12 A rebuild supersedes, so zpkgx fftw.org moves to it; a real version bump still dominates any number of rebuilds below it. Exact pins tell the two apart — =3.3.11 does not match 3.3.11_1, and the reverse — because a lock exists to say that nothing moved.
Absent means 0, which is Debian’s rule for its own revision and, until this was minted, the literal state of the registry: 0 of 1371 published version strings carried one.

data.a-manifest-alone-is-not-reproducible#A m:
Guix’s manual says it plainly: “to reproduce a profile bit-for-bit, manifests alone might not be enough”. The same names resolve differently against a different package set, so a manifest needs the channel revisions beside it.
And it matters more here than in Guix. A Guix manifest resolves deterministically once the channel revision is pinned, because the version is in the checkout. A zpkgx recipe’s versions: asks GitHub for tags at resolve time, so pinning the pantry commit is not enough: the same pantry resolves gnu.org/binutils to whatever the newest tag is the day you ask.
bk lock writes the answer down:
$ bk lock --platform linux/x86-64 -o base-toolchain.lock.hcl go-zpkg/base-toolchain set: go-zpkg/base-toolchain names 25 member(s) lock: 41 project(s) pinned → base-toolchain.lock.hcl lockfile_version = 1 bk = "v0.7.0" platform = "linux/x86-64" generated = "2026-10-05T09:10:39Z" pantry = "fd646990024e22f5752578cfdcfe2518b20c0797" overlay = "f8f6dcfd7b17410a6de780bdd58c81fbbb38d1b3" roots = ["go-zpkg/base-toolchain"] locked = { "curl.se" = { version = "8.17.0", spec = "sha256:5284d597c180…" } "gnu.org/bash" = { version = "5.3", spec = "sha256:…" } } The platform is in the header because it changes the answer: the same set locks to 41 projects on linux/x86-64 and 40 on darwin/aarch64 (github.com/besser82/libxcrypt is linux-only). A lock that did not say which platform it was taken on would be read as the other one’s.
data.a-set-is-an-ordinary-recipe#A set is an:
A recipe carrying members is a set:
# go-zpkg/base-toolchain members = { # clang, lld, compiler-rt — the compiler itself "llvm.org" = "*" # libc, crt objects and the dynamic loader "gnu.org/glibc" = "*" } Anything that takes a project name takes a set: bk closure go-zpkg/base-toolchain, bk factory --recipes go-zpkg/base-toolchain. A set is expanded at the root, before the dependency walk sees it, so nothing downstream has to learn the word.
The three systems that solved this agree on the shape, and Nix’s answer is the one taken:
Nix a tree is a derivation. buildEnv takes a list of packages and its output is a tree of symlinks. No new kind of object. Guix a manifest names packages; a profile is the tree it makes. Spack spack.yaml is the abstract set, spack.lock the concrete one. Because a set is an ordinary recipe, it is signed, attested, published and installed by everything that already does those things for a package — rather than a second kind of artefact to keep in step.
A set is unordered. All three of those manifests are: the order comes out of resolution, not out of the file.
data.checking-a-lock-later#Checking a lock la:
Cargo’s --locked and npm’s ci exist because a lock nobody verifies is a lock nobody can rely on. bk lock --check re-resolves and says what moved:
$ bk lock --check base-toolchain.lock.hcl lock: linux/x86-64 · 2026-10-05T09:10:39Z · 41 pinned, 2 hour(s) old lock: pantry revision differs: fd64699… → 9ab12cd… gnu.org/binutils 2.47 → 2.48 zlib.net spec 6a2d499db9ab → spec 90fae00e667c — same version, so something it is built FROM changed lock: 2 of 41 moved exit 0 nothing moved 1 something moved 2 the check could not be made at all The second line of that diff is the one a version-only lock cannot produce. It is what the spec hash is for.
Two deliberate kindnesses to whoever has to run this in CI:
a revision that moved is reported and is not fatal on its own. A pantry can move without moving any answer, and calling that drift would make the check cry wolf until nobody ran it. an unresolved project is kept apart from drift, for the mirror-image reason: a registry outage must not read as a pantry that changed. --check takes its roots, its platform and the revisions it expects from the file, and refuses a project name beside it — naming them twice would let the two disagree, and the answer would be about a different question from the one the file asks.
data.installing-a-lock#Installing a lock:
A lock that can be checked and built but not installed is a record of a build rather than a way to repeat it. zpkgm install --lock is the consumer end:
$ zpkgm install --lock seed.lock.hcl installed acme.org/tool v1.0.0 installed zlib.net v1.3.2 linked 2 binaries → /usr/local/bin Every pin is installed, not just the roots, and nothing is resolved. The roots are the only part of a lock a resolver could reconstruct — and reconstructing them is exactly what makes two installs of the same lock differ.
It refuses rather than guesses:
refused why a lock pinning recipes versions those are the newest the recipes can build, not the newest published: a fresh lock of curl.se for linux/aarch64 had 2 of its 5 pins ahead of the published bottles. Write an installable one with bk lock -runnable. A lock with no pinned field is a recipes lock — that is what every file written before the field existed holds a lock taken on another platform the platform changes the answer, and where versions happen to coincide it would otherwise succeed and give a set nobody locked --lock beside packages, -f, -p or -s a lock is the whole set, not a floor to add to That last row has a cost worth naming: -s/--from-scratch materialises the implicit glibc/libgcc_s/libstdc++/libatomic a scratch tree needs, and a lock does not pin them. So a FROM scratch image built this way is not yet reproducible from a lock alone — that needs those libraries pinned in the lock, which is a change to bk lock, not a flag here. The combination is refused instead of quietly installing more than the file describes.
data.naming-a-tree-and-pinning-it#Naming a tr: A recipe describes one package. Two things were missing above it: a way to name a group of packages, and a way to say which group — because the same names resolve differently tomorrow.
data.spec-because-a-version-is-not-enough-eit:
A version pins what upstream served. It does not pin the recipe: a build script edited in the pantry resolves to the same version and produces a different package.
Spack’s packaging guide names what a spec hash covers: "build, link, and run dependencies all affect the hash of Spack packages (along with sha256 sums of patches and archives used to build the package, and a canonical hash of the package.py recipes)". The last clause is the one copied here.
spec is a Merkle hash over the platform, the project, the resolved version, the parsed recipe and the spec hashes of its dependencies. Over the parsed value and not the file, so reformatting a recipe or rewriting its comments does not move it and changing what it says does.
data.what-a-lock-does-not-pin#What a lock doe: The output bytes. The spec hash covers the inputs, as Nix’s derivation hash and Spack’s spec hash do; an output digest is a different promise and is not made here. Every lock says so in its own header rather than letting a reader assume a guarantee that is not there.

data.a-gate-whose-default-answer-is-no#A gate:
bk origin --promotable is silent and exits 0 only when the provenance proves the host toolchain was unused. bk factory --mirror-from … --require-origin applies the same rule to every bottle it would copy, and refuses the rest:
❌ FAIL lz4.org 1.10.0: origin: not promotable: it was built with --bootstrap, so its compiler and shell came from the host distribution rather than from bottles ⛔ It requires an explicit 0 and treats every other answer as no, silence included. The recorded value is a tri-state rather than a boolean for exactly that reason: a boolean’s zero is false, which reads as “not a bootstrap”, so every bottle published before this existed would have claimed to be promotable.
The asymmetry is the whole argument. Refusing a good bottle costs a rebuild. Promoting a host-built one puts an unpinned distribution compiler’s output into the production registry under our signature. The default answer to “may I?” is no.
Three further properties, each a way this could have been built wrong:
The check runs before the download — nothing about having the tarball in hand makes a bottle more promotable. The verdict is carried, not restated. The facts belong to the build, and copying an artefact between registries does not change what built it; restating them would launder a verdict the copying run did not make, and would overwrite inputs-from. “I could not ask” is not “the answer was no.” An unreachable source registry is reported as a read failure naming the registry, never as a judgement about the bottle — a gate that folds the two together turns every network blip into a permanent verdict. A bottle published before bk v0.47.0 records no origin and therefore reads as not promotable. That is the intended answer rather than a regression: nothing is promoted that cannot be vouched for.
data.all-of-the-above-is-keyed-on-a-declared-:
Every number on this page is reached through the dependency graph. A bottle declares openssl.org ^3, the sweep asks OSV about the openssl version the catalogue says we carry, and a fix lands by rebuilding the openssl bottle. The whole mechanism rests on one assumption nothing was checking: that a declared dependency is the copy the artefact actually uses.
rpm.org/rpm-sequoia declares openssl.org ^3 on linux and links no libssl at all. A rebuild linked openssl 3.6.4 statically into the library — 4.2 MB to 12.6 MB, openssl’s own version banner inside the .so, nothing in DT_NEEDED.
A broken reference is visible: an unresolvable soname is something a sweep counts and bk unresolved reports. A vendored copy is invisible. The manifest still reads openssl.org ^3, so the scan asks about the right project at the right version and gets a true answer about a copy the bottle does not load. When openssl ships a fix, updating the openssl bottle does not change the bottle that embedded it, and its own version does not move either. There is nothing to compare.
bk unlinked asks the question backwards — which projects does a bottle declare and never link?
bk unlinked --platform linux/x86-64 rpm.org/rpm-sequoia bk unlinked --fail --platform linux/x86-64 < recipes.txt # as a gate rpm.org/rpm-sequoia declares openssl.org, which ships afalg.so, capi.so, legacy.so, libcrypto.so, libcrypto.so.3, libssl.so, libssl.so.3, loader_attic.so, padlock.so, and links none of them --platform matters more here than anywhere else on this page: the one confirmed case is published for linux and not for darwin, so a host-only command could not look at the very bottle the check was written for.
A finding is a candidate, and the output says so. Two different defects leave the same trace — a vendored copy, and an edge that is simply no longer needed — and only the second is harmless. The check reports direct edges only: a transitive dependency is one nobody promised to link, so a package that declares curl.se and links no openssl has done nothing wrong. A dependency that ships no shared library at all is never reported, because it cannot be linked and declaring it says something else — a program run at runtime, a data set like curl.se/ca-certs, an interpreter.
data.and-then-sunday-came#And then Sunday cam:
Those six versions are not all this registry publishes. Measured on 2026-11-01, openssl.org carries 72 tags across nine lines — 1.1.1, 3.0 and 3.1 as well — of which seven are end-of-life and two supported:
line verdict 1.1.1 ended 2023-09-11 (LTS) 3.0 ended 2026-09-07 (LTS) 3.1 ended 2025-03-14 3.2 ended 2025-11-23 3.3 ended 2026-04-09 3.4 ended 2026-10-22 3.6 ended 2026-11-01 3.5 supported to 2030-04-08 (LTS) 4.0 supported to 2027-05-14 A gate that reports a problem on the day it arrives has still left everyone on the abandoned line, so since zpkgx v0.30.0 the resolver acts on the verdict:
$ zpkgx --graph --platform linux/x86-64 +openssl.org@^3 openssl.org 3.5.8 It is a rank, not a filter. =3.6.4, ^3.6.4, ~3.6 and every lock still resolve to 3.6.4 — nothing supported satisfies them — and say so on stderr:
zpkgx: openssl.org 3.6.4 is on end-of-life release line 3.6 and nothing supported satisfies "=3.6.4"; using it Reproducibility outranks the preference: a lock that stopped resolving would be a worse defect than the one this fixes. So the preference changes an answer only where a supported candidate also satisfies the constraint, which is why it can never reach across a soname boundary — ^3 and ^4 share no satisfier.
The one answer that moves stays inside libssl.so.3, and its ABI cost was measured rather than assumed: 3.6.4 exports 6499 symbols and 3.5.8 6476, so 23 symbols are the whole of the risk (the new KEM CMS_RecipientInfo_kemri_*, the CRYPTO_*_array allocators, EVP_SKEY and friends). Across the ten heaviest consumers — curl.se, openssh.com, python.org, ruby-lang.org, postgresql.org, nodejs.org, php.net, erlang.org, openldap.org, libssh2.org — 45,601 imported symbols, none of them on that list. A sample of ten out of ~160 runtime dependents, not a proof about all of them.
ZPKG_DEPRECATED names a JSON file that replaces the built-in list, {"openssl.org": ["3.6"]}; {} turns the preference off. A named file that cannot be read or parsed is an empty list and a warning, never a silent fall back to the built-in one: naming a file is a statement about what you want, and substituting something else would hide the mistake behind behaviour that looks like it worked.
The build side is not there yet. bk resolves build-time dependencies through the same resolver and does not carry the list, so the factory still builds against 3.6.4 what zpkgx now runs against 3.5.8 (go-zpkg/bk#378). The list also still lives in the binary rather than in the signed catalogue, where it would be computed instead of committed (go-zpkg/bottle#179).
data.and-what-built-it#And what BUILT it, whi:
A signature says the bytes are ours. A source digest says what went in. Neither says whose compiler produced them — and on an architecture being brought up from nothing, that is the only question that matters.
Bringing one up needs two registries. The first generation takes its compiler and shell from the host distribution, because on an architecture with no bottles there is nothing else to take them from, so it publishes to a throwaway registry on the runner and never leaves it. Getting anything out of there needs one fact per bottle: was the host’s toolchain involved?
Measured on 2026-11-01, the registry could not answer:
$ bk buildenv --platform linux/s390x lz4.org 1.10.0 buildenv: lz4.org 1.10.0 (linux/s390x): the provenance records no build environment ⛔ An empty build environment is a hint, not a statement. A bootstrap build resolves no bottles, so its environment is empty — but so is a mirrored bottle’s, and so is every bottle published by an older bk. Three situations, one silence, and a gate cannot read a silence.
So the factory records the verdict, and bk origin reads it back:
$ bk origin --platform linux/s390x lz4.org 1.10.0 lz4.org 1.10.0 linux/s390x host toolchain used: no — built from bottles inputs resolved from: oci://ghcr.io/go-pkgx/packages inputs-from is the second fact, and it is the one no digest or signature can show: it distinguishes a bottle built against a seed’s loopback registry from one built against the production one.
data.and-where-a-recipe-declares-nothing-whic:
Verifying a declared sha: is worth having and reaches almost nothing. Measured on 2026-10-05 against a fresh pkgxdev/pantry: one recipe of 904 carries a sha: at all, and that one — openssl.org — points at ${{url}}.sha256, a file served by the same host as the tarball. It catches corruption in transit, which TLS already catches. It does not catch substitution: a host serving different bytes serves a matching .sha256 beside them.
So the source mirror grew a second job. It already kept every archive a build downloads, addressed by its SHA-256; it now also records which digest each URL served, and a later fetch that disagrees is refused:
fetch: this URL has served different bytes before: https://…/x-1.2.tar.gz now serves 2c26b4…, and served 9f86d0… before Trust on first use. It does not make an upstream trustworthy — it makes a change visible, which is the part nobody had.
A version bump is a first use, because the version is in the URL: a new release asks a question never asked before and is recorded rather than refused. That is why there is no --no-pin escape; the case it would serve does not arise.
The uncomfortable case is a mirror that cannot be asked. That is not an absent pin, and treating the two alike is how trust-on-first-use quietly becomes trust-every-time. They are distinguished, said out loud, and --source-pin-strict chooses which is fatal — warn and continue by default, because an unreachable registry is not evidence of tampering.
It is opt-in: --source-mirror is empty unless a run asks for it. Turning it on is safe rather than risky — the mirror’s existing contents carry only content tags, so the first pass records and only the second enforces.
Still missing, and it is a decision rather than a patch: openssl.org also declares sig: ${{url}}.asc, and nothing reads that field. It is the only control in the recipe format a compromised host could not forge — the signing key is not on www.openssl.org — and honouring it needs a key policy: whose key, pinned where, and what happens when a release is signed by a new one. A verifier that accepts any key proves only that somebody signed something.
data.end-of-life-is-not-a-cve#⛔ End-of-life i:
Everything above asks what is known to be wrong with this version. A release line upstream has abandoned has nothing known about it yet — and never will, because nobody is looking and no fix is coming. So the daily sweep returns a clean zero for a package whose upstream stopped issuing fixes years ago. bk eol asks the other question:
bk eol -product openssl 3.2.6 3.3.7 3.4.7 3.5.8 3.6.4 4.0.2 3.2.6 end-of-life line 3.2 ended 2025-11-23 3.3.7 end-of-life line 3.3 ended 2026-04-09 3.4.7 end-of-life line 3.4 ended 2026-10-22 3.5.8 supported line 3.5 supported until 2030-04-08 (LTS) 3.6.4 expiring line 3.6 ends 2026-11-01 4.0.2 supported line 4.0 supported until 2027-05-14 longest-supported openssl line: 3.5 (LTS), until 2030-04-08 Judged on 2026-10-29, when ^3 took the newest 3.x — 3.6, three days from the end of its line — while 3.5 LTS ran to 2030 and was already in the registry. Nothing in the CVE lane could say that.
A finding names its destination, because “3.6 ends on Sunday” is a problem and “3.5 is supported to 2030” is the next step. -fail makes it a gate and -within sets what counts as expiring.
data.it-asked-about-two-of-six#⛔ It asked abo:
The platform list was written into the workflow, and it named linux/x86-64 and darwin/aarch64 while the registry published six — linux/aarch64 among them, the largest here by bottle count. All four of the missing ones were clean, so the cost was coverage, not exposure; but an enumeration copied into a file freezes while the population grows.
The list is now derived. The index has always known which platforms exist — a platform that is not published is refused with platform not in index — and zpkgs catalog platforms asks it:
zpkgs catalog platforms # one per line, ready for --platform go run ./vulnsweep -pantry pantry -advisories advisories -store "$ZPKG_DIR" A seventh platform is covered the day it is published, by nobody’s decision. vulnsweep prints a line per platform, keeps going after a red one — a sweep that stops at the first reports one problem and hides the rest — and refuses to sweep nothing: an empty list, a list of noise, or a list it could not obtain is an error, never the clean zero this lane would otherwise print on the day the registry stops answering.
⭐ The first derived run found three real advisories, against vitejs.dev, on four platforms — two of which had never been scanned at all. We published vite 8.2.1 and the affected range is >= 8.2.0, < 8.2.4. The remedy was a rebuild at a version npm actually publishes above the fix boundary, which is worth checking: the 8.3 line is affected too, below 8.3.3.
-fail-on-new is a verdict, not a report: a finding already recorded has a decision behind it, and one that is not is a question with an answer. The job holds contents: read and never writes to the advisory tree — recording a decision stays a pull request, by a person.
data.known-vulnerabilities-asked-at-the-versi:
Signing says these are the bytes we built. It says nothing about whether those bytes are known to be vulnerable. That is a second question, and it is asked daily, for every platform we publish, by a scheduled job in go-zpkg/packages.
The whole design is in which question it asks. Ask OSV about each package as a whole and it returns every advisory that package has ever carried — 748 findings across 21 projects over this pantry on 2026-10-17, nearly all of them fixed long before anything we ship. Ask at the version the published catalogue says we carry, and skip outright the identities a platform carries no version of (2026-10-20):
platform asked at version unanswerable by OSV not asked (no bottle) findings linux/x86-64 133 1089 451 0 linux/aarch64 132 1104 437 0 darwin/aarch64 137 1082 452 0 darwin/x86-64 137 1074 462 0 windows/x86-64 94 461 1118 0 linux/s390x 1 28 1644 0 Each row adds to 1673, the identity count of the pantry — that sum is the control that no bucket is a silent drop. Unanswerable means an identity OSV is not keyed on: a repository or a CPE rather than a package in an ecosystem.
data.metadata-is-not-a-program-and-a-key-is-n:
Signatures cover the bytes. The strings beside them — a project’s name, its summary, the commands it provides, its versions and platforms — reach your terminal before any of that is checked, and they are written by people who are not you: an upstream recipe author, whoever wrote the lock you were handed, whatever registry ZPKG_DIST points at.
Measured, with a crafted lock:
$ zpkgx --lock esc.lock.hcl true | cat -v zpkgx: no version of zlib.net satisfies "=1.3.2\x1b[2K\r…" (available: 2); asked for by =1.3.2^[[2K^Mzlib.net 1.9.9 ✓ verified (requested) ESC[2K erases the line and \r returns the cursor, so on a terminal that line rubs itself out and reprints as something reassuring. The same hole was in the catalogue, where zpkgs ls printed versions straight through.
Three treatments, and which one applies depends on what the field is and who writes it:
field treatment why project name the whole file is refused a name becomes a URL and a path; a bad one means somebody wanted something summary, provides cleaned and shown cosmetic — refusing a catalogue over one paragraph would deny service for a typo version, platform in a lock the whole file is refused exactness is the entire point of a lock version, platform in a catalogue that entry is dropped, the file is kept, and the count is printed these come from an upstream recipe’s versions:, so refusing would hand any recipe author a switch that turns off zpkgs ls, search and every for everyone a tag from the registry skipped a registry is a configured endpoint A key can never be cleaned the way a caption is: a cleaned key would select something other than what it says. So it is refused or dropped, never silently repaired.
$ zpkgs catalog ~/.zpkg/catalog/darwin-aarch64.json 1908 project(s), 956 with dependencies, 2 hour(s) old If a catalogue ever carried an unreadable version, a third line would say so — 1 version string(s) were unreadable and are not listed. On a catalogue our own factory published it should never appear.
The allowlist was measured before it was written: across the two catalogues published on 2026-10-06, 2801 version strings use fifteen distinct runes and the longest is 19 bytes. What is accepted is deliberately wider than that, because a guard that refuses the ordinary case is a worse bug than the one it fixes.
data.supply-chain#Supply chain:
Every package in ghcr.io/go-pkgx/packages ships with the evidence needed to audit and trust it. Three artifacts are attached to each package as OCI referrers, so they travel with the image and are discoverable from its digest:
a CycloneDX SBOM — the package’s components and versions (go-attest/sbom); an in-toto SLSA provenance statement — how and from what the package was built; a cosign-style + minisign signature over the package (go-attest/sign).
data.the-field-that-lies#The field that would:
endoflife.date reports, for openssl:
{"name":"1.1.1","isEol":true,"eolFrom":"2023-09-11","isMaintained":true} {"name":"3.0", "isEol":true,"eolFrom":"2026-09-07","isMaintained":true} Both lines have been out of support for a while, and both say isMaintained: true — it reflects the paid extended support openssl sells. A check reading that field would report 1.1.1 as healthy, and this pantry has 32 bottles linking it. bk eol reads isEol and the date, never isMaintained; the field is not decoded into the type at all, so no later reader can reach for it by accident. An absent date is reported as unknown, never as supported: nobody committing to a date is not the same as a date far away.
data.the-trust-set#The trust set:
Signatures verify against a set of keys and a threshold of them, not against one key. The set contains, by default, the project’s own:
RWQ+rmH+fXy2iYr+gReQAOQtYWtH0A7UlxcAa2hpr+txNBwGqtpFsR6L The factory signs with the matching private key (held only as a CI secret).
variable effect ZPKG_TRUSTED_KEYS replaces the set — name:KEY, whitespace separated ZPKG_EXTRA_TRUSTED_KEYS adds to it ZPKG_TRUST_THRESHOLD how many distinct trusted keys must have signed (default 1) The shape is TUF’s — a role’s keys and a threshold, §4.3 — with its counting rule: a client “MUST NOT count more than one verified SIGNATURE from that KEYID towards the THRESHOLD” (§5.4.2). Without that rule a threshold of two is met by pushing one signature twice, which anyone who can push can do. The spelling of the key list is Nix’s trusted-public-keys, because an operator who has configured a binary cache already knows it.
data.two-builders-one-bottle#Two builders, on:
Two people who build the same inputs get the same bottle, hash and all. That is deliberate: an identity that varied with the builder could never be compared, and the collision is precisely the evidence. So you do not tell two builders apart by the artefact — you tell them apart by who signed it.
The registry holds one bottle and, potentially, several signature referrers over it. A threshold of 2 means I install nothing that a second builder did not independently reproduce.
export ZPKG_EXTRA_TRUSTED_KEYS='alice:RWQ…' export ZPKG_TRUST_THRESHOLD=2 zpkgm install lz4.org Nix requires one signature from one trusted key; Guix likewise checks a single authorised signature on a narinfo and compares servers out of band with guix challenge. A threshold makes that comparison a precondition of installing instead of an audit somebody runs afterwards.
The rebuilder’s side is two commands in zbk:
$ zbk reproduce yours.tar.gz theirs.tar.gz # do they agree, and how not? $ zbk sign -key you.sec -project fftw.org -version 3.3.11-h27o3… yours.tar.gz zbk sign pushes no bottle — re-publishing to add a signature is how you end up with two objects where the point was that there is one — and it refuses when the digests differ, printing both. That divergence is the finding: either the recipe is not reproducible, or one of the two machines is not what it claims.
Three rules worth stating, because each is a way the mechanism could have been quietly useless:
A signature from outside the trust set is counted and ignored, never an error. Anybody may sign a public artefact; if a stranger’s signature invalidated a bottle, invalidating any bottle would cost one push. A malformed signature referrer is counted, not skipped. Unsigned and signed, but the referrer is broken are different facts, and the second names a publishing bug. The signer name you read comes from your own trust set, never from the registry. The referrer carries only a key id, which is checkable — and which is used to decide which key to try first, never which may succeed.
data.verify-on-install#Verify on install:
The go-zpkg/bottle backend that both zpkgx and zpkgm import performs verification at install time:
every signature referrer on the bottle is collected, and the distinct trusted keys among them are counted against the threshold; ZPKG_VERIFY is on by default and fail-closed: a package with no signature, or too few that verify, is refused rather than installed. # refuses to install anything the trust set cannot vouch for ZPKG_DIST=oci://ghcr.io/go-pkgx/packages ZPKG_VERIFY=1 zpkgm install lz4.org Every path that brings bytes onto the machine goes through that check — not “every install”: every pull, the store cache included. A cache hit is re-checked against the signatures the registry advertises, because a cache is an optimisation and never an authority.
This closes the loop end to end: the factory signs and attests at publish time, and the consumer refuses to run anything it cannot verify.
data.what-a-decision-looks-like-and-how-far-i:
A decision is a dated event in advisories//advisories.yaml, and bk publish --advisories attaches it to the bottle as an OpenVEX v0.2.0 document, signed with everything else.
- id: MAL-2026-3020 events: - timestamp: 2026-10-11T10:29:00Z type: detection detected-version: 1.22.1 - timestamp: 2026-10-11T10:31:00Z type: false-positive-determination detected-version: 1.22.1 justification: component_not_present ⛔ detected-version is not paperwork. A purl names a version, so a VEX statement is a claim about a version — and the emitter will not restate the two statuses that tell a reader to stop looking, not_affected and fixed, about a version no event in the record names:
record determines not_affected for 1.22.1, bottle is 1.22.1 → not_affected + justification record determines not_affected for 1.22.1, bottle is 2026.9.1 → under_investigation + status_notes record names no version at all → under_investigation + status_notes Neither the justification nor the prose travels onto a downgraded statement: both were written about another artefact. affected is deliberately not downgraded — restating a warning for an unexamined version over-warns, which costs noise, while downgrading it would turn a warning into “we are looking into it”.
The gate and the document therefore read an absent version in opposite directions, on purpose: vulnfetch -fail-on-new treats a record that names no version as covering everything and stays green, because it interrupts us; the emitter treats it as covering nothing, because it reassures a stranger, and a stale “not affected” stops them looking. When in doubt do not interrupt ourselves; when in doubt do not reassure somebody else.
data.what-a-finding-is-not#⛔ What a finding i:
That last rule is a heuristic, and it has a floor worth stating before you read a list rather than after.
A program dependency whose bottle also ships a library is reported, and should not be. gnome.org/glib declares python.org, and its recipe says why — “several of the bins are scripts”. Nothing links libpython, but python’s bottle ships one, so the silence rule does not fire. The same happens for gnu.org/coreutils, whose bottle contains exactly one .so (libstdbuf.so, an LD_PRELOAD helper nobody links). Read those as declared for a program, not as defects.
A platform-split dependency is a real finding, not noise. gnome.org/glib also declares gnu.org/gettext: ^0.21 for every platform, and on Linux that is dead weight: libc.so.6 of glibc 2.44 exports gettext, dcgettext, dgettext, bindtextdomain, textdomain and ngettext itself, so nothing links -lintl there. GNU libintl is needed where libc lacks those — macOS. Ten projects in this pantry declare gettext unsplit; every Linux consumer installs it for functions already in libc.
The check sees DT_NEEDED, never dlopen. A plugin host that opens its providers at runtime links none of them by design, and will be reported. That is the one case where a finding can be both correct and uninteresting.
A short history is worth keeping beside the output, because it bears on how much a clean run is worth. The first sweep of a pantry with this command produced findings that measured the command: a soname was attributed to one owner when two projects shipped a file of that name (fixed in bk v0.44.1), and a real libfolly.so.0.58.0-dev was refused for its non-numeric version suffix while a libstdc++.so.6.0.33-gdb.py had earlier been counted as a library (v0.44.2: the name is a prefilter, the magic number decides). Both were caught by a finding that was not merely surprising but impossible — C++ libraries linking no C++ runtime. Use at least v0.44.2, and treat an impossible finding as a statement about the instrument.
data.what-went-in-not-only-what-came-out#What:
Those three describe the output. Until recently nothing recorded the input: of 1858 recipes with a source URL (measured 2026-09; re-counted 2026-10-05 as 1874 distributable URLs across 1899 recipes, reaching 233 distinct upstream hosts), exactly one declared a checksum, and none was verified. A source tarball that changed upstream produced a different package, correctly signed, attesting a URL rather than the bytes that came back from it.
The provenance now carries the source as a SLSA resolvedDependency — the archive’s SHA-256, or a git checkout’s commit:
"resolvedDependencies": [{ "uri": "https://github.com/ROCm/ROCR-Runtime/archive/refs/tags/rocm-7.2.4.tar.gz", "digest": {"sha256": "60532cd86edce5a603aa18df406ec1f5a3d18f0663d79b3b7822ff721c5a04ec"} }] It records the candidate URL that answered, which for a recipe listing mirrors is not always the first one — a build that fell through to a mirror and one that did not are different builds.
And where a recipe declares a sha: URL — the form the pkgx format already had and nothing read — the digest is verified. A mismatch fails the build rather than falling through to the next mirror: a build that quietly succeeded from a second host after the first served unexpected bytes would hide the one event that check exists to surface.

data.cost#What this costs:
Every bottle published before the break has to be rebuilt, not copied. A copy would carry the old internal paths, the old media types and no identity — it would move the defects rather than end them.
That is the whole reason the break happens now rather than later: the registry is the largest thing that would have to change, and it is cheaper to rebuild 1 967 projects once than to carry four inherited defects indefinitely and explain them to everyone who meets one.
data.namespaces#3. A vendor namespace that is:
Inherited: application/vnd.pkgx.bottle.layer.v1.tar+zstd, application/vnd.pkgx.source.layer.v1, dev.pkgx.source.uri.
The defect. Checked against upstream’s own corpus rather than assumed: pkgx distributes plain HTTPS tarballs from dist.pkgx.dev//// with .sha256sum and .asc beside them. It defines no OCI registry, no artifact type and no media type at all.
The OCI packaging is entirely ours — our factory invented it — and we had minted its names inside a vendor space whose owner never agreed to them. A name that looks like yours because you are the only one using it is not yours.
Our own keys had the same flaw one level down: the annotations were org.go-pkgx.*, and the rename turned them into org.go-zpkg.*. A reverse-DNS key is a claim on a domain, and nobody here has registered go-pkgx.org or go-zpkg.org. The rename carried an unbacked claim across rather than fixing it.
Now: application/vnd.go-zpkg.* for media types and io.github.go-zpkg.* for annotations — the reverse-DNS of a host that demonstrably answers, which is the convention OCI itself uses (org.opencontainers.image.*) applied honestly.
Read compatibility is asymmetric, and deliberately so. Layers are matched by their codec suffix (tar+zstd), never by the whole string, so both spellings read without the reader being told about either. Annotations are matched by exact key, so the older spellings are still read — including the intermediate org.go-zpkg.*, which shipped in five releases. The failure mode is why: a missed annotation key does not raise an error, it quietly concludes the bottle has no glibc flavour, no declared sonames and no recorded spec.
data.store-directory#2. Somebody else’s store:
Inherited: ~/.pkgx, and ~/.pkgx/config.hcl2 beside it.
The defect. ~/.pkgx is pkgx’s store. Once our runtime is zpkgx, upstream’s pkgx can be installed on the same machine and the same PATH — which is the entire reason for the rename. Two implementations writing one directory, under two layouts that are no longer even the same, is the collision the rename existed to remove, left in the one place it does the most damage.
Now: ~/.zpkg, ~/.zpkg/config.hcl2, and the store’s own marker file is .zpkg-platform. Nothing is migrated, on purpose: an existing ~/.pkgx is as much upstream’s as ours, and nothing in it says which bottles are whose. ZPKG_DIR=~/.pkgx keeps using the old one for anyone who wants that.
data.store-path#1. A store path keyed on the:
Inherited: ~/.pkgx//v/, with v1, v1.2 and v* aliases beside it. Upstream’s own documentation: “All packages are encapsulated in individual, versioned folders in ~/.pkgx.”
The defect. A path keyed on the version is a function of the version alone, so two builds of one version have one address. Installing the second met the first and the installer refused:
already holds other content … the bottle carries v3.3.11 That refusal is correct behaviour on a wrong layout. +cuda and ~cuda are not a sequence, there is no newer one, and nothing in the path said which was there.
It was not hypothetical. A rebuild is published as 3.3.11_1 and still unpacks to v3.3.11, so installing it into a store holding the original renamed onto an occupied directory, reported success, and installed nothing — the caller then ran a binary under a prefix that had never been created and got a bare no such file or directory.
Now: every installed tree is v-h. The hash is the build’s identity — platform, resolved version, the canonical form of the recipe, and the resolved prefix of every dependency. Two builds of one version are two directories, and each says which it is.
What survives, and why. v remains as a symlink, because it is in the published binaries. Read out of a real bottle:
$ otool -l …/zlib.net/v1.3.2/lib/libz.1.3.2.dylib name @rpath/zlib.net/v1.3.2/lib/libz.1.dylib Every binary that links zlib names that path. A store without it breaks all of them at load time, far from the cause. The hash goes on the real directory; the published path keeps resolving.
That seam closes when the registry is rebuilt: a bottle built with a hashed prefix carries the hash in its own @rpath references, and needs no alias at all.
data.the-break#The break:
Filiation says what go-zpkg inherits from pkgx and what pkgx cannot do by design. This page is the other half: the inherited things we removed, each with the defect that made removing it the cheaper option.
Nothing here is a complaint about pkgx. Every item is a reasonable decision for a tool that builds one version of each package once, and a wrong one for a tool that must hold two builds of one version and say which is which.
data.verification#4. A distribution that cann:
Inherited: https://dist.pkgx.dev, tarballs over HTTPS.
The defect. HTTPS authenticates the server, not the artifact: it says the bytes came from that host today, not that a particular build produced them.
Now: an OCI registry with a Sigstore signature and an SLSA provenance statement per bottle, and verification on by default — a bottle that cannot be verified is not installed, rather than installed with a warning. Upstream stays reachable as a choice: ZPKG_DIST=https://dist.pkgx.dev with ZPKG_VERIFY=0, which is the honest pairing said out loud.

That proves the module loads, instantiates and exits 0 — which is more than nothing, and less than working. Where a project takes real input the lanes pass it (yq, gojq, jj, tomljson, json2yaml, hcl2json all run against a fixture), and that is the standard to aim for when adding one.

data.a-wasip1-module-is-statically-linked-so-:
On every other platform a bottle is a node in a dependency graph. zpkgx walks it, installs the transitive closure, and sets up the environment the dynamic loader needs — DT_NEEDED on ELF, @rpath on Mach-O.
A wasm32-wasip1 module has no dynamic loader. Its libraries are linked into the module, so a single .wasm file is the whole program. This is not an optimisation of the install path; it is the absence of the thing the install path exists for.
Two consequences follow, and the second is a trap:
One file is enough. Fetching one bottle gives you something you can run. There is nothing else to resolve.
Do not resolve a wasip1/wasm closure. There is nothing to resolve, and a consumer that walks the deps anyway is doing work whose answer cannot matter.
Each entry is now read from the lane’s own recipe, so what it says about this platform is about this platform: lua.org declares only gnu.org/make, at build time, and the catalogue shows no runtime dep. Confirmed in the catalogue generated 2026-10-31T21:28:42Z.
It was not always so, and the shape of the defect is worth keeping. Until bk v0.46.0, bk catalog read a project’s fields from the pantry host recipe even when a platform lane had its own, so lua.org on wasip1/wasm listed gnu.org/readline — a package not published for the platform, and one the wasm build does not use at all, because it builds Lua’s generic ansi platform with no line editor. Nothing broke at run time, because nothing needs resolving, which is exactly why it went unnoticed. (go-zpkg/bk#376, fixed.)
provides is trustworthy again, and it is the half that mattered. It is what zpkgx -Q , zpkgs search by command name and the index are built from, so the same defect had sharper consequences there: in the catalogue of 2026-10-31T20:13Z, zlib.net listed no command although its bottle ships bin/minigzip.wasm — minigzip was published, runnable and unreachable by name — while filippo.io/age listed an age-keygen its bottle does not contain, sending anyone who asked for that command to a project that could not supply it. As of 21:28:42Z zlib.net names minigzip.
Two things from that episode are worth copying rather than forgetting. It was found by running every published module, not by parsing the catalogue — a consumer that only reads the catalogue cannot see either direction. And bk provides now exists to ask the question in the factory: it compares a published bottle’s actual bin/* against the provides the catalogue claims, and reports “listed, no file” and “file, not listed” as the separate failures they are.
data.bibliography#Bibliography: WASI preview1’s docs.md on the wasi-0.1 branch — the type layouts and the errno ordinals. wasi-libc’s __wasilibc_real.c — the import signatures as actually declared. docs.md writes path: string; only the real declarations show it lowered to a pointer and a length. wasi-libc’s wasip1.h — __WASI_ERRNO_NOSYS (UINT16_C(52)), which is how to check an errno ordinal was counted rather than guessed.
data.bytes-and-toolchain#⛔ A bottle’s bytes a:
The C/C++ lane resolves its toolchain — llvm.org, wasi-libc, compiler-rt.llvm.org/wasi, libcxx.llvm.org/wasi — at build time, and pins nothing. So rebuilding an unchanged recipe at an unchanged project version can produce a different module, and on 2026-10-31 it did: github.com/simdjson/simdjson v5.0.5 was republished with different bytes (the same 432 531 of them) and identical behaviour.
Measured at the same time, and worth knowing because it bounds the problem: zlib.net, lua.org and sqlite.org were rebuilt by the same runs and came out byte-identical. simdjson is the only C++ project of the four — the only one linking the floating libcxx.
Tracked in go-zpkg/packages#393, together with the separate finding that the publish step replaced an existing (project, version, platform) instead of skipping it. Until both are closed, a version does not pin bytes on this platform; a bk lock pins the version, and that is a weaker guarantee than it sounds.
data.finding-them#Finding them:
The catalogue is published per platform, so ask for this one:
zpkgs catalog update --platform wasip1/wasm zpkgs ls zpkgs ls --tree lua.org As with every other platform, zpkgs reads the local catalogue and nothing else — completion included — so this works offline once the catalogue is fetched. See Finding packages.
data.packages-that-run-in-a-webassembly-runti: wasip1/wasm is a platform of the factory like linux/x86-64 or darwin/aarch64: the same recipes, the same bk publish, the same registry at oci://ghcr.io/go-pkgx/packages, and the same catalogue. What differs is the one property that changes everything downstream.
data.running-one#Running one:
The reference runtime is wasmtime. Every bottle is run under it before it is published — the factory’s wasip1.yml (Go lane) and wasip1-c.yml (C/C++ lane) both do this, and a module that will not run is not published.
The invocation they use is the one to copy:
wasmtime run --dir=/ --env PWD="$PWD" ./sqlite3.wasm :memory: "select sqlite_version();" Both flags are load-bearing:
--dir=/ grants a filesystem. WASI has no ambient one: a module with no preopened directory cannot open any path, and the failure looks like a broken program rather than a missing grant.
⛔ And --dir=/ does not make a relative path work. Granting / does not put you in it: prog data.json can still fail to find data.json while prog "$PWD/data.json" succeeds. The factory’s own C/C++ smoke tests pass absolute paths for exactly this reason. If a module cannot see a file you are sure you granted, try the absolute path before suspecting the module.
--env PWD="$PWD" tells Go’s wasip1 runtime which preopen the working directory is in — the same thing $GOROOT/lib/wasm/go_wasip1_wasm_exec does. Without it a relative path resolves against nothing.
The arguments come after the module with no -- separator.
data.running-one-in-a-browser#Running one in:
The modules are the same bottles; a browser is just another WASI host. The landing page carries a playground that runs them client-side, at /playground/.
Two details of how it is built are worth knowing if you build something similar:
ghcr.io sends no CORS headers. A page cannot fetch a bottle from the registry; every browser refuses it, and no test on the page catches that because the page’s own tests do not cross an origin. The modules have to be served from the page’s own origin, which means a build step copies them there. An unimplemented syscall must not return 0. A host that answers “success” to a call it never implemented produces a run that looks exactly like one that worked. The playground’s host returns ENOSYS (errno 52 in preview1) and names the call on the page. That second point is why the playground’s host is checked by running the same modules under wasmtime and requiring the same stdout, the same stderr and the same exit status. It has already caught one difference worth repeating here: sqlite3 printed a box-drawing table where wasmtime printed 3.53.4, because wasi-libc’s isatty() answers from the filetype and rights that fd_fdstat_get reports, and a redirected stdout is UNKNOWN with FD_WRITE alone. A host that reports a terminal where the reference reports a pipe changes the output of programs that format for humans — silently, and only for some of them.
data.wasi-libc-gaps#What wasi-libc does not h:
The Go rejections above are a Go toolchain’s view. C and C++ hit a different wall, and these are the ones that cost real hours — each from a build that was attempted, not from reading a header:
the gap how it shows up no pipe() links, then fails at run time. xz reaches Error creating a pipe: Not supported from file_io.c’s self-pipe — the hardest kind, because the build is green signal.h refuses to compile an #error unless -D_WASI_EMULATED_SIGNAL is set, and then struct sigaction is still incomplete: sigaction, sigemptyset, sigfillset, sigprocmask, alarm are undeclared declared but not defined tmpfile, tmpnam, system link-fail as “undefined symbol” although the headers declare them (deprecated). They have to be stubbed to fail the way a sandbox would defined as ENOSYS fchmod, utime, chown are already in libc.a returning ENOSYS, so defining your own gives a duplicate symbol. Rename yours with -D instead of redefining chown/fchown undeclared while chown is simultaneously present in libc.a as the row above — declaration and definition disagree no dlopen any plugin or dynamic-module feature has to be configured off; it is why lua builds its generic ansi platform rather than posix setjmp/longjmp need a flag -mllvm -wasm-enable-sjlj -mllvm -wasm-use-legacy-eh=false, per WebAssembly/wasi-sdk’s SetjmpLongjmp.md. The standard instructions, not the legacy ones a 64 KiB default stack deep recursion traps rather than erroring. lz4 -d needed -Wl,-z,stack-size=8388608 The pattern across all of them: a green build says very little. Three of the eight above pass compilation and linking and fail only when the program runs, which is why every bottle on this platform is run under wasmtime before it is published.
data.what-will-not-build#What will not build:
A wasip1/wasm bottle is only published after the module has been run under wasmtime, so the lanes carry what works. This section is the other half: the candidates that were tried and rejected, with the cause. It is here because a documented “no, because X” is worth as much as a published bottle and saves the next person the same hours.
Every cause below is a compiler or linker error from a real attempt at the project’s latest tag, on GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm. They group into five families, and the families matter more than the names:
family what it needs that wasip1 has not seen in terminals and TTY ioctls unix.Termios, unix.IoctlGetWinsize, winsize ioctls, isatty, raw-mode echo control moby/term, reeflective/readline (GetSize), vbauerster/mpb, cheggaaa/pb (termutil.lockEcho), muesli/termenv (foregroundColor), fatih/color, logrus (isTerminal), bubbletea v2 the clipboard a desktop selection atotto/clipboard missing wasip1 backends a file-watching, SQL or socket implementation for this platform fsnotify.Watcher (via viper), modernc.org/libc (so modernc.org/sqlite), docker/go-connections (ForkLock, RawSockaddrUnix) file metadata and syscalls Stat_t fields and calls WASI does not carry djherbis/atime (Stat_t.Atime), u-root/ls (Stat_t.Rdev, unix.Major), go-git (isSymlinkWindowsNonAdmin), syscall.Mkfifo cgo a C toolchain at build time smacker/go-tree-sitter Two that belong to no family and are worth knowing:
A compiler limit, not a platform limit. miller fails with function too big … exceeds 65536 blocks in its generated parser. Nothing about WASI is involved; the wasm backend simply refuses a function that large. internal/robustio and azblob’s Mmb are build-constraint gaps in dependencies rather than anything a recipe can fix. The practical rule that falls out: a program that reads files or stdin and writes stdout ports almost for free; a program that draws on a terminal does not. fzf, less and nano are terminal programs and should be expected to fail, not attempted. Anything in Rust or C++ is a different lane entirely.

data.honest-limitations#Honest limitations: Native-Windows consumption only helps once Windows packages exist; until then, WSL2 remains the path for Windows users (linux binaries + linux packages). Packages whose upstreams have no Windows support won’t get packages — same opt-in reality as darwin. go-zpkg’s run closure-completion was built around ELF DT_NEEDED; the Windows equivalent (walking a PE import table for non-system DLLs) is a separate, smaller feature if/when shared-DLL packages appear.
data.proposal-to-pkgxdev#Proposal to pkgxdev: Add windows/x86-64 (+ aarch64) as first-class package slugs, built on the existing linux CI via llvm.org/mingw-w64, opt-in per recipe (platforms includes windows), starting with the packages that cross-build trivially (Go/Rust tools, single-file C tools). Package relocatability on Windows = colocate DLLs (no rpath) — a much smaller brewkit change than the linux relocation logic. go-zpkg provides a reference pure-Go client (zpkgx/zpkgm) that consumes Windows packages, and mirror to host them — so the ecosystem is testable independently of the reference Deno tooling.
data.the-two-halves-of-windows-support#The tw:
(A) Producing packages — an upstream (pkgxdev) concern. A pantry recipe would cross-build with llvm.org/mingw-w64 on the existing linux CI, e.g.
platforms: [linux, darwin, windows] # windows added build: dependencies: llvm.org/mingw-w64: '*' script: # for autotools/cmake projects: --host=x86_64-w64-mingw32, CC=x86_64-w64-mingw32-clang, … - $CC $CFLAGS foo.c -o {{prefix}}/bin/foo.exe Not every recipe ports cleanly (POSIX-only source, configure assuming a POSIX host, projects with no Windows story), so this is per-recipe, opt-in — exactly how darwin support already works. Pure-Go and Rust packages cross-compile to Windows almost for free.
(B) Consuming packages — the go-zpkg client side, which we control. Done and proven on a real windows-latest runner (go-zpkg v0.3.0):
bottle.Exec was syscall.Exec (UNIX-only; on Windows it’s a stub returning EWINDOWS). Split build-tagged: Windows spawns the target as a child with inherited stdio, waits, and exits with its code — a faithful exec analogue. goos() reports "windows"; bin/foo resolves to foo.exe. run on Windows: skip the ELF loader; set PATH (native separator) to the closure’s bin/lib dirs and exec the .exe. The CI job (go-zpkg/zpkgx, windows-latest) builds zpkgx.exe, fabricates a tiny Windows package (hello.exe) served over HTTP, and asserts that zpkgx.exe fetches and runs it (hello from zpkgx package (win)) and propagates a non-zero exit code — both pass on real Windows. mirror already runs on Windows unchanged (pure file+http), so a Windows box can host a mirror today.
Not yet done (follow-ups): zpkgm install shims are #!/bin/sh (need .cmd); the colocated-DLL case (a non-static shared dep) isn’t exercised because no such package exists yet.
data.tldr#TL;DR: Windows packages are feasible and, for most packages, simpler than the linux/darwin ones. zpkgx already ships the whole cross toolchain (llvm.org/mingw-w64). The blockers are (1) an upstream decision to build them and (2) a small runtime port of the client tools — not any deep technical wall.
data.what-was-proven-on-darwinarm64-from-this: # Finding Evidence 1 The cross-toolchain is already in the pantry. llvm.org/mingw-w64 (llvm-mingw) ships x86_64-w64-mingw32-clang and aarch64-w64-mingw32-clang (+ objdump/dlltool/…). So zpkgx’s own linux CI can cross-build Windows PE for both arches. zpkgx +llvm.org/mingw-w64 -- x86_64-w64-mingw32-clang … works 2 Cross-building a PE works. A C hello.c compiled to a valid PE32+ executable (console) x86-64, for MS Windows. file hello.exe → PE32+ 3 Leaf tools bundle nothing. The PE imports only Windows-provided DLLs — api-ms-win-crt-* (Universal CRT, present on Windows 10+) and KERNEL32.dll. objdump -p import table 4 C++ can be fully self-contained. clang++ … -static on a program produces a PE whose only imports are Windows DLLs — zero bundled libc++/libunwind/libwinpthread. objdump -p hi-static.exe
data.why-windows-packages-are-simpler-than-li:
The linux FROM-scratch work in this repo fought three things that do not exist on Windows:
No glibc package. Windows ships the C runtime (UCRT) as part of the OS. There is no gnu.org/glibc equivalent to mirror or to target. No rpath/RUNPATH dance. Windows resolves DLLs from the executable’s own directory first, then PATH. A package just colocates any shared DLLs next to the .exe (or in a lib/ dir put on PATH). No patchelf, no --dynamic-linker, no $ORIGIN. No loader indirection. There is no ld-linux to invoke explicitly; you exec the PE directly. So the package shapes are:
leaf C tool → a single .exe, no bundled libs. C/C++ with static libs (-static) → a single self-contained .exe. shared-lib deps → the .exe + the dependency DLLs colocated in the package.
data.zpkgx-windows-packages-feasibility-study: Date: 2026-07-31 · zpkgx has no Windows packages today (every dist.pkgx.dev//windows/* returns 404). This studies whether that can change, with a working cross-build proof, and proposes a path.
